title: Dürer’s edge-unfolding conjecture
open: Can every convex polyhedron be cut along some spanning tree of its edges and unfolded into a single non-overlapping planar polygon? Formally, decide whether Dürer’s edge-unfolding conjecture — commonly formalized through Shephard’s 1975 question — is true, or exhibit a counterexample.
status: The problem is commonly formalized through Shephard’s 1975 question. Substantial special cases and affine-unfolding results — notably Ghomi (2014), *Affine unfoldings of convex polyhedra*, arXiv:1305.3231 — do not settle the original conjecture.
solved_when: Either a proof that every convex polyhedron admits a non-overlapping edge unfolding is given, or an explicit convex polyhedron is constructed for which every spanning tree of edges yields an overlapping unfolding.
why: A solution would clarify when rigid three-dimensional structures admit collision-free flat manufacturing layouts, and would resolve the fundamental question of whether edge cuts always suffice for polyhedral flattening.
key_works: Ghomi (2014), *Affine unfoldings of convex polyhedra*, arXiv:1305.3231.

title: Certifying infeasibility in narrow-passage problems
open: When a sampling-based planner fails to find a path, is the task truly infeasible or is there a narrow passage it simply has not discovered? Develop practical planners that distinguish an undiscovered narrow passage from genuine infeasibility, with explicit geometric assumptions and independently checkable infeasibility certificates.
status: Sampling planners can fail to find paths that exist, while exact geometric methods give stronger conclusions but face scaling barriers; the obstacle is tractability, not the absence of decidability results.
solved_when: A planner exists that, under stated geometric assumptions, either finds a path or produces an independently checkable certificate of infeasibility, so that failure is no longer indistinguishable from an undiscovered passage.
why: It prevents indefinite retries and false declarations that a manipulation task is impossible, turning planner failure into an actionable conclusion.
key_works: Orthey, Chamzas, and Kavraki (2024), *Sampling-Based Motion Planning: A Comparative Review*, arXiv:2309.13119.

title: Real-time global certificates for trajectory optimization
open: Can a robot compute a globally valid optimality — or bounded-suboptimality — certificate for a nonlinear, robot-scale trajectory within its operational control deadline?
status: Semidefinite relaxation approaches provide certificates for structured polynomial problems; extending their tractable range remains open. Key works: Kang et al. (2024/2025), *Fast and Certifiable Trajectory Optimization*, arXiv:2406.05846.
solved_when: A method produces globally valid optimality or bounded-suboptimality certificates for robot-scale nonlinear trajectories within an operational control deadline.
why: It replaces confidence in a local optimizer with auditable trajectory-quality guarantees.
key_works: Kang et al. (2024/2025), *Fast and Certifiable Trajectory Optimization*, arXiv:2406.05846.

title: Certifiable SLAM with unknown data association
open: Can we jointly infer landmark correspondences and robot trajectories — with useful global certificates — when appearances are ambiguous and outliers are present?
status: SE-Sync certifies structured synchronization problems; however, certification with unknown correspondences is substantially harder than optimizing a correctly associated graph. Key work: Rosen et al. (2019), *SE-Sync: A Certifiably Correct Algorithm for Synchronization over the Special Euclidean Group*, arXiv:1612.07386.
solved_when: An algorithm exists that jointly estimates data association and trajectory and returns a global optimality certificate for the joint problem, remaining valid under ambiguous appearances and outliers.
why: It prevents confidently wrong maps caused by perceptual aliasing, where distinct landmarks look alike and corrupt the inferred map.
key_works: Rosen et al. (2019), *SE-Sync: A Certifiably Correct Algorithm for Synchronization over the Special Euclidean Group*, arXiv:1612.07386.

title: Consistent distributed SLAM with unknown correlations
open: Can a team of intermittently communicating robots fuse their maps without double-counting shared information, when the correlations between their estimates are unknown because their processing histories and learned features overlap? Formally, is there a distributed fusion rule that remains consistent (never overconfident) under uncertain inter-robot dependencies?
status: Distributed estimation offers conservative fusion strategies, but these tend to sacrifice informativeness; efficient, informative fusion under uncertain dependencies remains difficult. Key work: Placed et al. (2023), *A Survey on Active Simultaneous Localization and Mapping*, arXiv:2207.00254.
solved_when: A distributed map-fusion method is exhibited that is provably consistent despite unknown cross-robot correlations, and remains efficient and informative rather than merely conservative.
why: It would let fleets build shared maps collaboratively without the artificial overconfidence that corrupts estimates when common information is counted twice.
key_works: Placed et al. (2023), *A Survey on Active Simultaneous Localization and Mapping*, arXiv:2207.00254.

title: Physical resolution of the Painlevé paradox
open: When rigid-body models with Coulomb friction predict either no consistent motion or several possible motions, what actually happens in the physical world? Establish experimentally validated rules that select the realized outcome, especially in three-dimensional multicontact systems.
status: The paradox dates to the nineteenth century; compliance-based analyses clarify important cases without supplying a universal selection rule (Champneys and Várkonyi, 2016, *The Painleve paradox in contact mechanics*, arXiv:1601.03545).
solved_when: A selection rule for the indeterminate or inconsistent cases exists, is validated against physical experiments, and extends to three-dimensional multicontact systems.
why: It determines whether the contact behavior produced by a simulation corresponds to a real robot–environment interaction, rather than to an artifact of an ill-posed rigid-body model.
key_works: Champneys and Várkonyi (2016), *The Painleve paradox in contact mechanics*, arXiv:1601.03545.

title: Correct gradients through contact-mode changes
open: Can we compute mathematically justified gradients for trajectories that pass through contact-mode changes — contacts being created or broken — rather than sensitivities that merely reflect artifacts of a smoothing parameter? In other words, is there a notion of derivative for nonsmooth contact dynamics that remains useful and valid across mode transitions?
status: Randomized smoothing and differentiable contact methods provide partial approaches, but fidelity at nonsmooth transitions remains a central issue. Key works include Le Lidec et al. (2021), *Leveraging randomized smoothing for optimal control of nonsmooth dynamical systems*, and Montaut et al. (2023), *Differentiable Collision Detection: a Randomized Smoothing Approach*.
solved_when: A method yields sensitivities for trajectories involving contact creation or breaking that are provably correct (mathematically justified) and independent of smoothing-parameter artifacts, rather than optimizing smoothing artifacts.
why: Without such gradients, gradient-based policy and mechanism optimization over contact-rich dynamics can converge to artifacts of the simulator's smoothing rather than true physical improvements; correct sensitivities make that optimization physically meaningful.
key_works: Le Lidec et al. (2021), *Leveraging randomized smoothing for optimal control of nonsmooth dynamical systems*; Montaut et al. (2023), *Differentiable Collision Detection: a Randomized Smoothing Approach*.

title: Continual skill acquisition without regression
open: How can a robot acquire new physical skills over time while provably preserving the capabilities it already has, including rare but consequential regressions that surface only after later updates?
status: The LIBERO benchmark (Liu et al. (2023), *LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning*, arXiv:2306.03310) measures lifelong knowledge transfer, but dependable retention across changing real-world tasks remains a larger, unmet target.
solved_when: A method exists that adds new skills while passing an evaluation protocol that detects rare but consequential regressions in old capabilities after each update, with dependable retention across changing real-world tasks rather than benchmark tasks alone.
why: It prevents a useful robot from becoming less reliable as it learns, so that learning can continue in deployment without eroding earlier competence.
key_works: Liu et al. (2023), *LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning*, arXiv:2306.03310.

title: Certifying online policy updates
open: Can a robot be allowed to improve its policy during deployment while a certification mechanism guarantees that every accepted update preserves specified safety constraints and essential capabilities?
status: Runtime assurance and barrier-based filtering provide partial protection (see Ames et al. (2019), *Control Barrier Functions: Theory and Applications*, arXiv:1903.11199, and Luckcuck et al. (2019), *Formal Specification and Verification of Autonomous Robotic Systems*), but certifying an evolving complete behavior remains more demanding.
solved_when: A deployed robot can adopt online policy updates such that each accepted update is certified to preserve the specified safety properties and essential capabilities, covering the complete behavior rather than isolated components.
why: It reconciles continual learning with dependable operation: without it, robots must either forgo in-field improvement or accept unverified behavioral changes.
key_works: Ames et al. (2019), *Control Barrier Functions: Theory and Applications*, arXiv:1903.11199; Luckcuck et al. (2019), *Formal Specification and Verification of Autonomous Robotic Systems*.

title: Complete classification of mobile spatial 6R linkages
open: Which spatial closed chains of six revolute joints can actually move? The goal is a complete classification of mobile 6R linkages — including exceptional and degenerate families — under clearly stated equivalence relations.
status: Bond theory and algebraic methods establish important families and necessary conditions; paradoxically mobile linkages remain a rich classification frontier. See Schicho (2022), *And Yet It Moves: Paradoxically Moving Linkages in Kinematics*, arXiv:2004.12635; DOI:10.1090/bull/1721.
solved_when: Every mobile spatial 6R linkage belongs to an explicitly described family, and every family in the classification is provably mobile, with equivalences between families formally defined.
why: A complete classification would expand the catalog of compact closed-chain mechanisms available to robot designers and settle the long-standing puzzle of paradoxically mobile linkages.
key_works: Schicho (2022), *And Yet It Moves: Paradoxically Moving Linkages in Kinematics*, arXiv:2004.12635; DOI:10.1090/bull/1721.

title: Tenfold longer-lived artificial muscles
open: Can artificial muscles be made to last ten times longer in useful actuation cycles than today's best, without sacrificing anything else? Formally, the target is at least a 10× increase in useful actuation cycles at matched strain, stress, frequency, and packaging volume, with performance retained even after partial damage.
status: HASEL actuators demonstrate muscle-like performance and electrical self-healing (Acome et al. (2018), *Hydraulically amplified self-healing electrostatic actuators with muscle-like performance*, DOI:10.1126/science.aao6139), but mechanical lifetime under matched workloads is a separate target that remains unmet. Related directions include dielectric fatigue and self-healing polymer mechanics.
solved_when: An actuator demonstrates at least 10× more useful actuation cycles than current devices while matching strain, stress, frequency, and packaging volume, and maintaining performance after partial damage.
why: A solution would make soft actuation operationally competitive, removing lifetime as the barrier that keeps artificial muscles out of long-duration applications.
key_works: Acome et al. (2018), *Hydraulically amplified self-healing electrostatic actuators with muscle-like performance*, DOI:10.1126/science.aao6139.

title: Independent control of many field-driven microrobots
open: How can many microrobots be steered independently when all of them respond to the same small number of global magnetic, acoustic, or electric actuation channels? Formally, the question is whether a shared global input field can be decomposed or exploited (via heterogeneity, geometry, or dynamics) so that each robot's trajectory is controlled independently despite the common input.
status: External-field actuation is effective for small devices, but the shared global inputs create controllability and interference constraints that currently limit independent control. Related theoretical threads include ensemble controllability and underactuated population control. Key work: Sitti et al. (2015), *Biomedical Applications of Untethered Mobile Milli/Microrobots*, DOI:10.1109/JPROC.2014.2385105.
solved_when: A control scheme is established that achieves independent, simultaneous control of multiple microrobots sharing few global actuation channels, overcoming the interference constraints that shared inputs impose.
why: It unlocks coordinated microscale tasks — with individual robots playing distinct roles — rather than only collective motion of the swarm.
key_works: Sitti et al. (2015), *Biomedical Applications of Untethered Mobile Milli/Microrobots*, DOI:10.1109/JPROC.2014.2385105.

title: Autonomous approach to an initially unknown small body
open: Can a spacecraft approach, characterize, select a landing site on, and land on an asteroid or comet it has never seen before, without a ground team resolving each major uncertainty along the way? Formally, this asks for end-to-end onboard autonomy spanning estimation, mapping, site selection, and touchdown.
status: Integrated autonomous estimation has been studied in realistic blind simulations, but end-to-end operational autonomy remains a stronger, unmet target. Key work: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies Toward Greater Autonomy for Deep Space Missions*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.
solved_when: A mission-demonstrated (or high-fidelity blind-simulation-validated) system autonomously completes approach, characterization, landing-site selection, and landing on an initially unknown small body, with no ground intervention required to resolve major uncertainties.
why: It would make small-body exploration scalable to many targets, rather than requiring a ground team per mission.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies Toward Greater Autonomy for Deep Space Missions*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.

title: Dressing across garments and mobility limitations
open: Can a robot safely dress a person it has not been fitted for — accounting for varied body shapes, pain constraints, involuntary motion, and limited mobility — using garments it has not encountered before, without making harmful contact? Formally, the goal is a dressing controller that generalizes across both users and garments while guaranteeing harm-free contact.
status: Deep haptic model-predictive control has demonstrated gown dressing with human participants, as in Erickson et al. (2018), *Deep Haptic Model Predictive Control for Robot-Assisted Dressing*, arXiv:1709.09735; DOI:10.1109/ICRA.2018.8460656, but broad coverage across garments and users remains open.
solved_when: A robot system demonstrates dressing of users with diverse body shapes, mobility limitations, pain constraints, and involuntary motion, using unfamiliar garments, while preventing harmful contact throughout the task.
why: Dressing is a high-value daily assistance task for people with limited mobility; a general solution would make assistive dressing robots practical beyond carefully controlled scenarios.
key_works: Erickson et al. (2018), *Deep Haptic Model Predictive Control for Robot-Assisted Dressing*, arXiv:1709.09735; DOI:10.1109/ICRA.2018.8460656.

title: Sharp finite-budget guarantees for optimal sampling-based planning
open: Can a sampling-based motion planner be given a stopping rule that certifies, after a finite number of samples, that its returned path is within a specified cost of optimal? The goal is matching upper and lower bounds on the required sample budget that explicitly account for the environment's clearance, dimension, and obstacle geometry.
status: PRM* and RRT* established asymptotic optimality in 2011 [Karaman and Frazzoli (2011), *Sampling-based Algorithms for Optimal Motion Planning*, arXiv:1105.1186], but asymptotic convergence alone does not provide this instance-sensitive stopping certificate.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are proved on the number of samples needed to achieve a given path-cost error, with the bounds explicitly depending on clearance, dimension, and obstacle geometry.
why: It lets planners report defensible quality-versus-computation guarantees, turning asymptotic optimality into an instance-sensitive stopping certificate.
key_works: Karaman and Frazzoli (2011), *Sampling-based Algorithms for Optimal Motion Planning*, arXiv:1105.1186.

title: Kinodynamic planning without a reliable steering function
open: Can we build a motion planner with strong completeness and convergence guarantees for high-dimensional nonlinear systems, when connecting two states requires solving a numerical boundary-value problem that may not converge reliably? In other words, what theory covers the case where the steering function itself is untrusted?
status: Sampling and optimization methods cover important restricted dynamics; the difficult residual combines drift, unstable dynamics, state constraints, and bounded computation. See Orthey, Chamzas, and Kavraki (2024), *Sampling-Based Motion Planning: A Comparative Review*, arXiv:2309.13119.
solved_when: A planner is given for kinodynamic systems with high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics, together with provable completeness and convergence guarantees that hold despite the boundary-value solver failing or returning unreliable answers; no quantitative budgets (round counts, exponents, error tolerances) are specified, so establishing such guarantees for this setting is the criterion.
why: It would extend dependable planning beyond well-behaved systems to agile aircraft, underactuated machines, and contact-rich systems, where such guarantees are currently missing.
key_works: Orthey, Chamzas, and Kavraki (2024), *Sampling-Based Motion Planning: A Comparative Review*, arXiv:2309.13119.

title: Planning across singular constraint manifolds
open: How can a motion planner cross regions where the constraint manifold itself changes dimension — such as kinematic singularities or contact changes — without violating constraints or losing completeness? Formally, the goal is to construct planners that traverse changing-dimensional or singular configuration sets while maintaining constraint satisfaction and completeness guarantees.
status: Constraint-manifold sampling is established, but transitions at kinematic singularities and changing contact constraints remain more demanding than planning on a smooth fixed manifold. Related perspectives come from stratified spaces and numerical algebraic geometry; see Zhang et al. (2024/2025), *Motion Planning for Robotics: A Review for Sampling-based Planners*, arXiv:2410.19414.
solved_when: A planner is constructed that provably traverses singular or changing-dimensional constraint sets while maintaining constraint satisfaction and completeness guarantees.
why: It supports closed-chain manipulation, coordinated carrying, and mechanism assembly, where singular and changing contact configurations are unavoidable.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2024/2025), *Motion Planning for Robotics: A Review for Sampling-based Planners*, arXiv:2410.19414.

title: Replanning guarantees under unpredictable obstacle motion
open: When can a robot guarantee both safety and eventual task completion when obstacles move unpredictably — outside any prediction model — but under explicit bounds on their speed and behavior?
status: Dynamic planners and local avoidance methods exist, but their guarantees depend strongly on environmental assumptions and on the availability of safe waiting or escape states. Zhang et al. (2024/2025), *Motion Planning for Robotics: A Review for Sampling-based Planners*, arXiv:2410.19414.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the obstacle speed and behavior limits (and environmental conditions) under which a planner preserves both safety and eventual task completion; no quantitative targets are stated in the record.
why: It separates deadlocks that are genuinely unavoidable from failures that are artifacts of the planner, telling practitioners when to blame the environment rather than the algorithm.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2024/2025), *Motion Planning for Robotics: A Review for Sampling-based Planners*, arXiv:2410.19414.

title: Collision-query lower bounds for learned planners
open: Establish when learned geometric priors can provably reduce collision-checking complexity, and when distribution shift forces any planner back to worst-case exploration.
status: Learned sampling can accelerate favorable instances; the target is a matched information-theoretic account of its limits, not another favorable benchmark average. Key works: Karaman and Frazzoli (2011), *Sampling-based Algorithms for Optimal Motion Planning*, arXiv:1105.1186; Orthey et al. (2024), *Sampling-Based Motion Planning: A Comparative Review*. Related lines include distribution-free learning lower bounds and oracle complexity.
solved_when: A matched information-theoretic account exists giving lower bounds on collision-checking complexity under learned priors and distribution shift, showing which speedups provably survive unfamiliar environments and which cannot beat worst-case exploration.
why: It identifies which planning speedups can survive unfamiliar environments, separating genuine gains from benchmark-specific artifacts.
key_works: Karaman and Frazzoli (2011), *Sampling-based Algorithms for Optimal Motion Planning*, arXiv:1105.1186; Orthey et al. (2024), *Sampling-Based Motion Planning: A Comparative Review*.

title: Automatically discovering sound planning abstractions
open: Can a system automatically discover planning abstractions — predicates and operators — whose symbolic plans are guaranteed to remain executable under continuous dynamics, even under uncertainty and changes in object geometry?
status: Neuro-symbolic skill learning demonstrates useful abstractions, as in Silver et al. (2023), *Learning Neuro-Symbolic Skills for Bilevel Planning*, arXiv:2206.10680; soundness and completeness across new task distributions remain stronger targets.
solved_when: A method exists that learns such predicates and operators with symbolic plans provably executable (sound) under the specified conditions of continuous dynamics, uncertainty, and varying object geometry.
why: It removes extensive hand-written domain engineering without sacrificing executability.
key_works: Silver et al. (2023), *Learning Neuro-Symbolic Skills for Bilevel Planning*, arXiv:2206.10680.

title: Rearrangement planning with irreversible actions
open: How should a planner reason about cluttered environments when actions like moving, discarding, cutting, or fastening an object can permanently eliminate future options? Formally, the challenge is to plan effectively while explicitly tracking recoverability of the world state.
status: Integrated task-and-motion planning handles many rearrangement domains, as surveyed in Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*, arXiv:2010.01083; however, destructive actions and uncertain reversibility complicate standard search assumptions.
solved_when: A planning method exists that handles rearrangement domains with destructive actions, explicitly tracking which state changes are irreversible, without the standard search assumptions that break under uncertain reversibility.
why: It enables repair, demolition, cooking, and assembly tasks to be automated without premature irreversible mistakes.
key_works: Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*, arXiv:2010.01083.

title: Belief-space task and motion planning at household scale
open: Can a household robot jointly choose its sensing, manipulation, and navigation actions while explicitly maintaining uncertainty over object existence, poses, affordances, and human intent?
status: Belief-space formulations and restricted demonstrations exist; large hybrid belief spaces remain a scaling obstacle. Key work: Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*, arXiv:2010.01083.
solved_when: A planner demonstrates integrated belief-space task and motion planning at household scale, handling uncertainty over object existence, poses, affordances, and human intent without collapsing uncertain scene interpretations into fixed facts.
why: It prevents a robot from treating uncertain scene interpretations as established facts, so actions are chosen with awareness of what is actually known about the environment and the human.
key_works: Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*, arXiv:2010.01083.

title: Planning with previously unknown tools
open: Can a robot learn to use a tool it has never seen before through limited safe interaction, and then fold what it learns into a physically executable multistep plan? Formally, the goal is to infer a novel tool's operational constraints and make them available to a planner that produces physically realizable action sequences.
status: Skill libraries support known tools and learned operators; discovering new tool semantics and their continuous constraints remains a broader target. Key work: Silver et al. (2023), *Learning Neuro-Symbolic Skills for Bilevel Planning*, arXiv:2206.10680.
solved_when: A robot facing a previously unknown tool can, via a bounded amount of safe interaction, infer the tool's operational constraints and use them to synthesize a physically executable multistep plan that accomplishes a task requiring that tool.
why: It frees robots from a fixed catalog of end-effectors and fixtures, letting them solve tasks in environments whose tooling was not anticipated at design time.
key_works: Silver et al. (2023), *Learning Neuro-Symbolic Skills for Bilevel Planning*, arXiv:2206.10680.

title: Recovery-aware symbolic plans
open: Can a symbolic planner automatically generate plans that come with executable recovery branches for realistic execution failures — slips, dropped objects, failed insertions, and changed human instructions — instead of assuming every action succeeds?
status: Task-and-motion frameworks integrate discrete and continuous feasibility, but systematic recovery synthesis remains distinct from nominal plan generation.
solved_when: A task-and-motion planning system produces nominal plans together with contingency branches covering slips, dropped objects, failed insertions, and changed human instructions, such that the branches are executable at run time.
why: Converts a successful demonstration into a usable autonomous workflow.
key_works: Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*, arXiv:2010.01083.

title: Resource-aware concurrent manipulation
open: Can we plan multiple robots to act concurrently in a shared workspace when success depends on coupled resources — temporary supports, shared tools, battery reserves, human access — and on deadlines whose timing is uncertain at planning time? Formally, the question is how to extend integrated symbolic-and-continuous planning to handle interacting temporal and physical resource constraints under stochastic execution times.
status: PDDLStream (Garrett, Lozano-Pérez, and Kaelbling (2020), *PDDLStream: Integrating Symbolic Planners and Blackbox Samplers via Optimistic Adaptive Planning*, arXiv:1802.08705) links symbolic planning with continuous sampling; the residual open difficulty is adding interacting temporal and physical resource constraints on top of that integration. Related formalisms include stochastic resource-constrained scheduling and temporal constraint networks.
solved_when: A planning method exists that produces concurrent multi-robot plans respecting temporary supports, shared tools, battery reserves, human access, and deadline constraints under uncertain execution times — i.e., the symbolic–sampling integration carries the interacting temporal and physical resource constraints.
why: It would let fleets do genuinely useful parallel work instead of serialized toy workflows, since current pipelines force sequencing whenever resources and time interact.
key_works: Garrett, Lozano-Pérez, and Kaelbling (2020), *PDDLStream: Integrating Symbolic Planners and Blackbox Samplers via Optimistic Adaptive Planning*, arXiv:1802.08705.

title: Calibrated black-box feasibility samplers
open: How can a task planner reason soundly when its feasibility samplers — such as learned grasp generators or numerical inverse-kinematics solvers — sometimes fail even when a feasible solution exists?
status: Black-box streams provide a practical interface for integrating samplers into planning, as in Garrett, Lozano-Pérez, and Kaelbling (2020), *PDDLStream*, arXiv:1802.08705; however, distinguishing sampler inadequacy from genuine physical infeasibility remains an important unresolved residual.
solved_when: A planning framework exists that treats feasibility samplers as black boxes yet correctly distinguishes sampler inadequacy from physical infeasibility, so that high-level reasoning remains sound despite hidden numerical failures.
why: Without this, silent numerical failures inside samplers can corrupt the planner's high-level conclusions, leading it to reject problems that are actually solvable.
key_works: Garrett, Lozano-Pérez, and Kaelbling (2020), *PDDLStream*, arXiv:1802.08705.

title: Optimal allocation of symbolic and geometric search
open: How should a planner divide its finite computation among candidate symbolic plans, the continuous parameter searches they require, sensing actions, and local optimization — and can that division come with performance guarantees?
status: Optimistic adaptive planning provides a concrete partial approach; universally effective allocation across heterogeneous search components is not established. Related directions include metareasoning, algorithm portfolios, and bandits with dependent arms; Garrett, Lozano-Pérez, and Kaelbling (2020), *PDDLStream*, arXiv:1802.08705 is a key work.
solved_when: An allocation strategy is given, across symbolic plans, continuous parameter searches, sensing actions, and local optimization, with stated performance guarantees under a finite computation budget.
why: It prevents a planner from exhausting its entire budget refining a single unproductive plan skeleton before considering alternatives.
key_works: Garrett, Lozano-Pérez, and Kaelbling (2020), *PDDLStream*, arXiv:1802.08705.

title: Place recognition under simultaneous appearance and structural change
open: Can a robot recognize a place it has visited before when everything about the scene has changed at once — seasons, layout, viewpoint, and repeated structure — while still refusing to claim a match for places it has never seen?
status: Contemporary place-recognition research addresses multiple change factors individually; their conjunction, along with calibrated rejection of unseen places, remains demanding. Yin et al. (2025), *General Place Recognition Survey: Towards Real-World Autonomy*, arXiv:2405.04812.
solved_when: A place-recognition system demonstrates robust recognition under the simultaneous occurrence of seasonal appearance change, structural/layout alteration, viewpoint shift, and repeated architectural patterns, together with calibrated rejection of genuinely unseen places.
why: It is what makes return visits reliable over months and years of operation, rather than only across single controlled change factors.
key_works: Yin et al. (2025), *General Place Recognition Survey: Towards Real-World Autonomy*, arXiv:2405.04812.

title: Persistent identity in dynamic maps
open: How can a robot's map preserve the identity of objects over long periods of time — objects that move, disappear and later return, split into parts, or become occluded — without mistaking a temporary absence for a permanent change in the environment?
status: The robust-perception SLAM agenda explicitly extends beyond static geometry; persistent object identity requires additional temporal semantics. The key work is Cadena et al. (2016), *Past, Present, and Future of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping: Toward the Robust-Perception Age*, DOI:10.1109/TRO.2016.2624754.
solved_when: A mapping system is achieved that maintains persistent object identities through motion, occlusion, disappearance, return, and splitting, while distinguishing temporary absence from permanent environmental change.
why: It supports locating possessions, tracking maintenance, and reasoning about changes over time.
key_works: Cadena et al. (2016), *Past, Present, and Future of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping: Toward the Robust-Perception Age*, DOI:10.1109/TRO.2016.2624754.

title: Semantic-map uncertainty that remains calibrated
open: Can a semantic map carry joint, calibrated uncertainty over its labels, geometry, and object relationships — including the correlations that arise when all observations pass through a shared learned perception model? Formally, is there a representation in which these coupled uncertainties are propagated consistently rather than treated as independent scores?
status: Semantic mapping itself is established (Cadena et al. (2016), *Past, Present, and Future of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping*, DOI:10.1109/TRO.2016.2624754), but treating neural confidence scores as calibrated map probabilities remains unjustified without additional modeling.
solved_when: A mapping formulation exists whose stated uncertainties over semantic labels, geometric quantities, and inter-object relations are jointly calibrated, accounting for correlations induced by the shared perception model, with that calibration demonstrable under the map's stated assumptions.
why: Without jointly calibrated uncertainty, downstream risk-sensitive planning on semantic maps is built on numbers that do not mean what they claim; with it, a planner can trade off perception-derived risk soundly.
key_works: Cadena et al. (2016), *Past, Present, and Future of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping*, DOI:10.1109/TRO.2016.2624754.

title: Bounded-memory lifelong mapping without catastrophic forgetting
open: Can a robot maintain a map of a continually changing environment within a fixed memory budget while still preserving the information needed for future localization, navigation, and change detection? Formally, is there a compression scheme whose memory footprint is bounded independently of the robot's lifetime and whose retained map provably supports these downstream tasks?
status: Lifelong autonomy motivates map maintenance and forgetting; the sharper target is task-aware retention with quantified future performance. Kunze et al. (2018), *Artificial Intelligence for Long-Term Robot Autonomy: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.05196. Related threads include streaming compression and sufficient statistics for nonstationary processes.
solved_when: A mapping scheme is given that operates under a fixed memory budget for a nonstationary environment, together with quantified guarantees on future localization, navigation, and change-detection performance.
why: It prevents map storage and maintenance costs from growing without bound, which is a prerequisite for genuinely lifelong autonomy rather than autonomy bounded by disk space.
key_works: Kunze et al. (2018), *Artificial Intelligence for Long-Term Robot Autonomy: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.05196.

title: Active SLAM with truthful information gain
open: Select exploration actions using information-gain estimates that remain accurate when future measurements are correlated, association is uncertain, and the observation model is learned.
status: Active SLAM has mature formulations, but tractable approximations can change which exploration action appears most valuable. See Placed et al. (2023), *A Survey on Active Simultaneous Localization and Mapping: State of the Art and New Frontiers*, arXiv:2207.00254.
solved_when: An active SLAM method exists whose information-gain estimates provably remain accurate under correlated future measurements, uncertain data association, and learned observation models.
why: It prevents robots from spending expensive exploration effort that reduces an internal uncertainty metric without improving real knowledge.
key_works: Placed et al. (2023), *A Survey on Active Simultaneous Localization and Mapping: State of the Art and New Frontiers*, arXiv:2207.00254.

title: Registration certificates under structured adversarial outliers
open: When can point cloud registration be certified as correct if the incorrect correspondences are not independent random outliers but form coherent competing alignments? A formal answer would give practical identifiability conditions and certification thresholds under such structured adversarial ambiguity.
status: TEASER (Yang, Shi, and Carlone (2021), *TEASER: Fast and Certifiable Point Cloud Registration*, arXiv:2001.07715) demonstrates extreme outlier robustness in tested settings, but structured ambiguity requires stronger assumptions than an outlier percentage alone.
solved_when: Identifiability conditions and quantitative certification thresholds are established for registration under structured (coherent competing alignment) outliers, showing what assumptions beyond an outlier percentage suffice for certification.
why: It clarifies when apparently robust registration can still select the wrong physical alignment, which is exactly the failure mode a certificate is supposed to rule out.
key_works: Yang, Shi, and Carlone (2021), *TEASER: Fast and Certifiable Point Cloud Registration*, arXiv:2001.07715.

title: Transparent-object geometry under uncontrolled illumination
open: Can a robot recover the geometry — with usable uncertainty estimates — of transparent, refractive, or partially liquid-filled objects under backgrounds and lighting it has not seen before, so that the shapes are accurate enough to grasp and manipulate?
status: ClearGrasp (Sajjan et al. (2020), *ClearGrasp: 3D Shape Estimation of Transparent Objects for Manipulation*, arXiv:1910.02550) demonstrated learned transparent-object reconstruction; reliable generalization beyond its training and sensing assumptions remains a broader target.
solved_when: A system reconstructs manipulation-relevant shape with calibrated uncertainty for transparent, refractive, and partially liquid-filled objects, and generalizes reliably beyond its training and sensing assumptions to unfamiliar backgrounds and illumination.
why: It would make manipulation of glassware, packaging, and laboratory objects dependable, where current methods fail outside narrow conditions.
key_works: Sajjan et al. (2020), *ClearGrasp: 3D Shape Estimation of Transparent Objects for Manipulation*, arXiv:1910.02550.

title: Event-camera calibration during operation
open: Can an event camera be calibrated while it is still running, so that changing event thresholds, timing offsets, temperature effects, and camera motion are estimated jointly and online, without stopping to perform a laboratory calibration?
status: Event-based vision provides low-latency sensing, and its measurement model and calibration differ materially from ordinary frame cameras; no online self-calibration method of this kind is recorded. Key context: Gallego et al. (2022), *Event-based Vision: A Survey*, arXiv:1904.08405.
solved_when: A method exists that jointly estimates these parameters during operation, with no interruption of the sensor's normal use for calibration procedures.
why: It preserves reliable perception during high-speed and high-dynamic-range operation, where drift in these parameters would otherwise silently corrupt event-based measurements.
key_works: Gallego et al. (2022), *Event-based Vision: A Survey*, arXiv:1904.08405.

title: Tenfold lower-energy event-based perception
open: Can an event-based perception pipeline achieve at least a tenfold reduction in total sensing-plus-computation energy relative to a matched frame-based pipeline, without sacrificing detection latency or navigation reliability?
status: Event sensors provide sparse measurements that promise energy savings, but no system-level demonstration exists; any credible saving must account for preprocessing, idle power, and downstream inference costs. Gallego et al. (2022), *Event-based Vision: A Survey*, arXiv:1904.08405.
solved_when: A demonstrated system shows a ≥10× reduction in total energy (sensing plus computation, including preprocessing, idle power, and downstream inference) against a matched frame-based pipeline while meeting the specified detection latency and navigation reliability targets.
why: A tenfold energy reduction would substantially extend the endurance of small autonomous robots, whose runtime is typically limited by perception power rather than actuation or batteries alone.
key_works: Gallego et al. (2022), *Event-based Vision: A Survey*, arXiv:1904.08405.

title: Identifiable tactile force reconstruction
open: When can the full contact force distribution and frictional stresses on a tactile sensor be uniquely recovered from its tactile images, given sensor hysteresis and unknown object compliance? A formal answer would characterize the conditions on contact geometry, material response, and loading under which this inverse problem is well posed.
status: GelSight sensors measure detailed contact geometry and support force estimation, but universal inversion of tactile images to contact forces remains blocked by mechanical ambiguities. Key work: Yuan, Dong, and Adelson (2017), *GelSight: High-Resolution Robot Tactile Sensors for Estimating Geometry and Force*, DOI:10.3390/s17122762. Related problems include inverse elasticity and uniqueness of boundary-traction reconstruction.
solved_when: A characterization — sufficient and, ideally, necessary conditions — exists under which distributed contact forces and frictional stresses are uniquely identifiable from tactile images in the presence of sensor hysteresis and unknown object compliance, together with a reconstruction method meeting that characterization.
why: It would allow force-sensitive manipulation using tactile sensing alone rather than relying on wrist force measurements, and would resolve the mechanical ambiguities that currently block universal inversion of tactile images.
key_works: Yuan, Dong, and Adelson (2017), *GelSight: High-Resolution Robot Tactile Sensors for Estimating Geometry and Force*, DOI:10.3390/s17122762.

title: Tactile sensing that survives wear and contamination
open: Can a robot's tactile sensing stay accurately calibrated as its sensing surfaces are abraded, punctured, oiled, dusted, cleaned, and eventually replaced? The goal is an engineering design or procedure that maintains calibrated tactile performance through the full wear-and-replacement cycle of a sensing skin.
status: High-resolution optical tactile sensors, such as Yuan, Dong, and Adelson (2017), *GelSight*, DOI:10.3390/s17122762, demonstrate rich tactile measurements, but lifetime stability remains a separate, unmet deployment requirement.
solved_when: A tactile sensing system demonstrably maintains its calibrated performance through abrasion, punctures, oil exposure, dust, cleaning, and skin replacement, rather than degrading as surfaces age.
why: Without it, dexterous manipulation policies degrade as the contact surfaces they were trained and calibrated on wear out; solving it keeps deployed systems reliable over their working life.
key_works: Yuan, Dong, and Adelson (2017), *GelSight*, DOI:10.3390/s17122762.

title: Multiple-source chemical localization in turbulent air
open: Can a moving robot determine how many chemical sources there are, where they are, and how strongly each emits, when the sensors are cross-sensitive, the air is turbulent in an unknown way, and the sources themselves change over time? Formally, this asks for joint inference of the source count, spatial distribution, and time-varying emission rates from in-situ measurements under uncharacterized turbulent advection–diffusion.
status: Gas-source localization has been studied since the 1990s, but source mixtures, sensor memory, and uncontrolled flow remain central difficulties. A survey of the field is Francis et al. (2022), *Gas source localization and mapping with mobile robots: A review*, DOI:10.1002/rob.22109.
solved_when: An algorithm using mobile, cross-sensitive sensors recovers the number, positions, and time-varying emission rates of the sources to specified accuracy in an unknown turbulent flow, with guarantees or reproducible validation across changing source conditions.
why: It would enable leak detection and environmental monitoring by robots, finding and quantifying hazardous releases without exposing people to the chemicals.
key_works: Francis et al. (2022), *Gas source localization and mapping with mobile robots: A review*, DOI:10.1002/rob.22109.

title: Open-set audition during robot motion
open: Can a robot in motion separate its own motor, impact, and structural noise from its audio input while still preserving unfamiliar environmental sounds that were never enumerated during training? Formally, this asks for open-set ego-noise suppression that does not assume a closed inventory of ambient sound classes.
status: A September 2026 preprint, Shoda et al. (2026), *Open-Set Ego-Noise Separation for Legged-Robot Audition via Annotation-Free Adaptation and Pretrained-Model Transfer*, arXiv:2609.07440, addresses open-set ego-noise separation; cross-platform transfer and preservation of rare safety-relevant sounds remain stronger evaluation targets.
solved_when: A method removes motor, impact, and structural noise during robot motion while preserving environmental sounds absent from the training set, evaluated on open-set sounds — including rare safety-relevant ones — and shown to transfer across robot platforms.
why: It lets robots hear people, mechanical failures, and events outside their visual field rather than masking them as noise.
key_works: Shoda et al. (2026), *Open-Set Ego-Noise Separation for Legged-Robot Audition via Annotation-Free Adaptation and Pretrained-Model Transfer*, arXiv:2609.07440.

title: Active sensor placement without disturbing the phenomenon
open: How can a robot plan its measurements when its own presence — through airflow, heat, vibration, illumination, or contact — alters the very phenomenon it is trying to observe? Formally, the challenge is to design active sensing strategies that jointly model and compensate for these platform-induced disturbances while still gathering informative data.
status: Mobile chemical sensing explicitly encounters platform-induced measurement effects; correcting them jointly with exploration remains challenging. Key works: Francis et al. (2022), *Gas source localization and mapping with mobile robots: A review*, DOI:10.1002/rob.22109.
solved_when: A planning method exists that explicitly accounts for the robot's self-induced effects (airflow, heat, vibration, illumination, contact) on the measured phenomenon, and produces measurements that remain scientifically interpretable — demonstrated, at minimum, on mobile chemical sensing where such platform effects are known to occur.
why: It makes robotic environmental measurements scientifically interpretable; without it, data collected by mobile platforms is confounded by the robot's own disturbance of the phenomenon, undermining the conclusions drawn from it.
key_works: Francis et al. (2022), *Gas source localization and mapping with mobile robots: A review*, DOI:10.1002/rob.22109.

title: Simultaneous-impact laws for many contacts
open: Can we predict the post-impact motion of a rigid-body system when several contacts occur nearly simultaneously, using impact parameters that are experimentally identifiable and yield controlled sensitivity to microscopic timing details?
status: Different impact and time-stepping formulations can produce different outcomes, so model selection requires more than numerical stability. Key works: Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372.
solved_when: A simultaneous-impact law is formulated whose parameters can be identified from experiments and whose predicted post-impact outcomes remain well-conditioned with respect to microscopic timing variations across many contacts.
why: Accurate simultaneous-impact prediction improves modeling of falls, grasp closure, bouncing objects, and legged landing.
key_works: Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372.

title: Friction models with history, wear, and contamination
open: Can we find compact friction models that predict how contact transitions among sticking, sliding, and rolling change as surfaces accumulate history, wear, and contamination during use? Formally, the goal is a low-dimensional friction law whose parameters evolve with surface state and that anticipates mode transitions rather than assuming fixed, freshly calibrated coefficients.
status: Coulomb-style models remain useful approximations, and contact-model comparisons — e.g., Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372 — expose consequential modeling choices.
solved_when: A compact model demonstrably predicts transitions among sticking, sliding, and rolling on surfaces whose state has evolved through use, outperforming fixed-parameter Coulomb-style baselines in contact-model comparisons.
why: It supports reliable robotic manipulation beyond freshly calibrated laboratory surfaces, where real-world wear and contamination otherwise break the assumptions of standard contact models.
key_works: Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372.

title: Quantifying simulator-induced policy bias
open: How much does the choice of contact solver, regularization scheme, or friction approximation bias the policy that a learning agent ultimately selects—not just the error of the simulated trajectories it trains on? Can we derive bounds relating these modeling decisions to policy-level deviations?
status: Comparative contact studies show that modeling decisions matter; policy-level transfer guarantees require an additional theory. Key work: Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372.
solved_when: A quantitative bound is established that relates changes in contact solver, regularization, or friction approximation to the change in the learned policy (beyond trajectory-level simulation error), for a stated class of contact models and learning setups.
why: Without such bounds, agents can silently exploit simulator-specific contact artifacts and transfer poorly to hardware; the theory would underpin policy-level transfer guarantees.
key_works: Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372.

title: Contact-rich simulation at industrial particle counts
open: Can we build a contact-rich simulator that handles granular material, cables, cloth, and rigid tools simultaneously, with force predictions validated well enough for engineering use, at speeds that make it practical for planning and learning pipelines? In other words, a unified simulator whose accuracy and throughput match the demands of real robotic control rather than offline analysis.
status: Existing deformable-object simulators cover selected material classes, but coupled heterogeneous contacts create additional accuracy and scaling demands. Lin et al. (2020), *SoftGym: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning for Deformable Object Manipulation*, arXiv:2011.07215, benchmarks deformable object manipulation.
solved_when: A simulation system demonstrates coupled heterogeneous contact (granular media, cables, cloth, rigid tools together) with validated force predictions, running at speeds suitable for planning and learning at industrial particle counts.
why: It directly enables automation of excavation, recycling, food handling, and bulk-material manipulation, where validated contact forces and fast simulation are prerequisites for control.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), *SoftGym: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning for Deformable Object Manipulation*, arXiv:2011.07215.

title: Convergent rigid limits of compliant contact
open: When a robot makes contact modeled by increasingly stiff compliance, does the simulated motion actually settle down to a single rigid-body trajectory, or can different damping and regularization choices select different limits? A formal characterization is sought of when the rigid limit of compliant contact models exists, is unique, and is independent of the regularization details.
status: Painlevé-type behavior shows that the rigid limit can be singular; a broad classification for robot-relevant multicontact systems remains open. Champneys and Várkonyi (2016), *The Painleve paradox in contact mechanics*, arXiv:1601.03545.
solved_when: A classification is given for robot-relevant multicontact systems that identifies the conditions under which stiff compliant models converge to a unique rigid-contact trajectory and the conditions under which different damping or regularization choices yield distinct limits.
why: It determines whether increasing simulator stiffness actually improves physical fidelity, rather than silently steering the simulation toward an arbitrary trajectory.
key_works: Champneys and Várkonyi (2016), *The Painleve paradox in contact mechanics*, arXiv:1601.03545.

title: Tenfold faster certified collision detection
open: Can certified collision detection be made an order of magnitude faster end-to-end? Formally, achieve at least 10× lower end-to-end collision-checking cost on a public, difficult geometry suite, while preserving conservative guarantees on matched hardware.
status: GJK++ accelerates established collision-detection machinery; a broad certified system-level target must include preprocessing and worst-case behavior. Key work: Montaut et al. (2024), *GJK++: Leveraging Acceleration Methods for Faster Collision Detection*.
solved_when: A system demonstrates at least 10× lower end-to-end collision-checking cost on a public, difficult geometry suite, with conservative guarantees preserved and hardware matched for comparison.
why: A solution frees computation for larger searches and shorter control cycles.
key_works: Montaut et al. (2024), *GJK++: Leveraging Acceleration Methods for Faster Collision Detection*.

title: Fragility-aware grasping of unknown objects
open: Can a robot select and execute grasps on objects whose fragility is unknown, inferring fracture, crushing, and surface-damage thresholds without ever performing a damaging trial?
status: General grasping and manipulation have advanced, as surveyed in Billard and Kragic (2019), *Trends and challenges in robot manipulation*, DOI:10.1126/science.aat8414; however, unknown fragility introduces a separate hidden-state and safe-exploration problem that remains open.
solved_when: A grasp-selection and execution method demonstrably infers hidden fragility thresholds and grasps unknown objects while avoiding damage, with no damaging trials used during inference.
why: It unlocks safe robotic handling of produce, antiques, electronics, and thin packaging.
key_works: Billard and Kragic (2019), *Trends and challenges in robot manipulation*, DOI:10.1126/science.aat8414.

title: In-hand manipulation across unfamiliar object families
open: Can a single robotic hand reorient and reposition an object it has never seen before, coping with unfamiliar mass distribution, friction, compliance, and contact geometry? Formally, the goal is a manipulation system that generalizes across object families rather than a fixed, known object, and that maintains control despite the uncertain contact and dynamics conditions those families present.
status: Learned dexterous in-hand manipulation has delivered important sim-to-real results, notably OpenAI et al. (2018/2020), *Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation*, arXiv:1808.00177; however, breadth across object families and recovery remain stronger targets than current systems achieve.
solved_when: A one-handed system demonstrably reorients and repositions previously unseen objects across unfamiliar object families, handling unknown mass distributions, friction, compliance, and contact geometry, with recovery behavior robust enough to be counted among its validated capabilities.
why: Success would reduce dependence on fixtures, regrasp stations, and specialized tooling, letting a single hand adapt to new objects instead of relying on task-specific hardware.
key_works: OpenAI et al. (2018/2020), *Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation*, arXiv:1808.00177.

title: Predicting slip before irreversible grasp loss
open: Can a robot sense that a grasp is beginning to slip early enough to intervene, across contact materials that change, without either over-squeezing or retraining sensors for each new material?
status: Tactile sensing exposes local deformation at contacts, but transferring early-warning rules across different contacts remains an open challenge distinct from detecting an object that is already slipping. Related ideas come from early-warning signals in dynamical systems and sequential change detection. See Li et al. (2025), *The Developments and Challenges towards Dexterous and Embodied Robotic Manipulation: A Survey*, arXiv:2507.11840.
solved_when: A detection method is demonstrated that identifies incipient slip before irreversible grasp loss, generalizes across changing contact materials without sensor-specific retraining, and avoids excessive grip force.
why: It prevents dropped objects while limiting damage to delicate items and energy wasted on unnecessary grip force.
key_works: Li et al. (2025), *The Developments and Challenges towards Dexterous and Embodied Robotic Manipulation: A Survey*, arXiv:2507.11840.

title: Manipulation through prolonged visual occlusion
open: How can a robot complete contact-rich manipulation using only touch and proprioception when its own hand, tool, or a container blocks the camera for an extended period? Formally, the goal is a control and estimation scheme that maintains reliable state tracking and task completion through prolonged visual occlusion.
status: Dexterous systems already integrate multiple sensing modalities, but reliable state tracking through long occlusions remains a demanding residual, as surveyed in Li et al. (2025), *The Developments and Challenges towards Dexterous and Embodied Robotic Manipulation: A Survey*, arXiv:2507.11840.
solved_when: A system completes contact-rich operations during extended visual occlusion using touch and proprioception, with reliable state tracking maintained throughout the occluded interval.
why: It would enable reaching into bags, assembling inside housings, and operating under furniture — tasks where vision is inherently blocked during the critical contact phase.
key_works: Li et al. (2025), *The Developments and Challenges towards Dexterous and Embodied Robotic Manipulation: A Survey*, arXiv:2507.11840.

title: General-purpose extrinsic dexterity
open: How can a robot deliberately exploit its environment — tables, walls, edges, gravity, and temporary supports — to manipulate objects in ways its hand alone cannot achieve? The goal is a general-purpose method for planning and controlling such extrinsic dexterity, rather than task-specific tricks.
status: It is known that environmental contacts can extend manipulation capability, but planning their use under uncertain friction and geometry remains difficult. See Billard and Kragic (2019), *Trends and challenges in robot manipulation*, DOI:10.1126/science.aat8414.
solved_when: A robot system can use environmental contacts and supports to complete manipulations that exceed its hand’s intrinsic capabilities across varied objects and scenes, robustly handling uncertain friction and geometry.
why: It would let simpler, cheaper hands perform substantially more capable manipulation, trading expensive mechanisms for clever use of the environment.
key_works: Billard and Kragic (2019), *Trends and challenges in robot manipulation*, DOI:10.1126/science.aat8414.

title: Tool-use transfer across handle and working-end changes
open: Can a robot that has learned a tool-using skill apply it to a new tool whose handle, functional tip, leverage, and required contact forces all differ from the training examples? More formally, this asks for generalization across changes in tool geometry at both the handle and the working end, rather than only across handle variations.
status: General manipulation policies learn useful task families, but identifying the causal role of each tool geometry remains an open generalization target. A representative foundation is Chi et al. (2023), *Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion*, arXiv:2303.04137.
solved_when: A policy trained on a set of tool examples executes the skill successfully on a new tool with a different handle, functional tip, leverage, and required contact forces, without retraining.
why: It avoids retraining a separate policy for every screwdriver, brush, utensil, or scraper a robot might encounter.
key_works: Chi et al. (2023), *Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion*, arXiv:2303.04137.

title: Bimanual coordination under asymmetric uncertainty
open: How can two robot hands coordinate their actions when one hand's sensing or visibility of the shared object is degraded? A complete answer should cover load transfer, handoffs, and response to unexpected motion of the object while one side operates under poor visibility or sensing.
status: ALOHA (Zhao et al. (2023), *Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware*, arXiv:2304.13705) demonstrates fine-grained learned bimanual tasks, but robust coordination under asymmetric failures requires additional mechanisms beyond what it provides.
solved_when: A bimanual control or learning scheme is demonstrated that maintains robust coordination — through load transfers, handoffs, and unexpected object motion — even when one hand has substantially degraded visibility or sensing, without decomposing the task into independent arm motions.
why: It enables large-object handling and delicate operations that cannot be decomposed into independent arm motions.
key_works: Zhao et al. (2023), *Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware*, arXiv:2304.13705.

title: Mobile manipulation without hidden environmental preparation
open: Can a mobile manipulation system complete full household workflows — moving across rooms, through unmodified environments — without any hidden environmental preparation? That is, without prepositioned objects, cleared approaches, fixed furniture poses, or human resets between subtasks.
status: Mobile ALOHA demonstrates learned whole-body mobile manipulation; removing preparation and reset assumptions remains a stronger deployment target. Key work: Fu, Zhao, and Finn (2024), *Mobile ALOHA: Learning Bimanual Mobile Manipulation with Low-Cost Whole-Body Teleoperation*, arXiv:2401.02117.
solved_when: A system demonstrates complete household workflows across multiple rooms under none of the following aids: prepositioned objects, cleared approaches, fixed furniture poses, or human resets between subtasks.
why: It measures useful autonomy rather than performance on carefully staged episodes, which is what deployment actually demands.
key_works: Fu, Zhao, and Finn (2024), *Mobile ALOHA: Learning Bimanual Mobile Manipulation with Low-Cost Whole-Body Teleoperation*, arXiv:2401.02117.

title: Recovering hidden cloth topology
open: Can a robot infer the hidden structure of cloth — its folds, layers, openings, and self-contact regions — from partial observations, well enough to distinguish cloth states that look similar on the surface but differ operationally underneath?
status: Deformable-object research identifies occlusion and state representation as persistent challenges, and visible surface reconstruction alone is known to be insufficient. Key work: Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767.
solved_when: A method exists that, from partial observations of cloth, recovers the hidden topology (folds, layers, openings, self-contacts) and reliably distinguishes visually similar but operationally different cloth states.
why: It underpins practical fabric tasks — dressing, laundry, bedding, and fabric manufacturing — where acting on the wrong hidden state leads to failure even when the visible surface looks correct.
key_works: Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767.

title: Reliable single-layer separation
open: Can a robotic system reliably pick exactly one layer from a stacked or folded textile, despite adhesion, static charge, porosity, and uncertain thickness? Formally, the goal is a construction: a single-layer separation method robust to these disturbances.
status: Cloth manipulation has many successful task-specific systems, but detecting accidental multilayer pickup and recovering reliably remains a distinct, unsolved problem. See Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767.
solved_when: A demonstrated system that picks exactly one layer from stacked or folded textiles under adhesion, static charge, porosity, and uncertain thickness, and reliably detects and recovers from accidental multilayer pickup.
why: Reliable single-layer separation is a prerequisite for automating garment production, laundry sorting, and sterile textile handling.
key_works: Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767.

title: Knot and tangle manipulation with hidden crossings
open: Can a robot autonomously identify and untangle a previously unseen cable or rope configuration when crossings and endpoints are partially hidden from view, without tightening the knot or damaging the material?
status: Cable manipulation has specialized methods, but topology changes, occlusion, and tension constraints have so far only been addressed with joint reasoning rather than a unified solution. Key work: McKenna and Oyekan (2026), *A Perspective on Open Challenges in Deformable Object Manipulation*, arXiv:2602.22998.
solved_when: A manipulation system demonstrates untangling of unseen cable or rope configurations under partial occlusion of crossings and endpoints, while avoiding both knot tightening and material damage.
why: Reliable untangling under occlusion directly serves household cable management, surgical suturing, fishing gear handling, and industrial wiring.
key_works: McKenna and Oyekan (2026), *A Perspective on Open Challenges in Deformable Object Manipulation*, arXiv:2602.22998.

title: Cable routing with connector and bend constraints
open: Can a robot autonomously route a flexible cable through clips and confined passages so that every physical constraint is respected? Formally, find a routing strategy that satisfies bend radius, twist, tension, connector orientation, and serviceability requirements throughout the installation.
status: Existing deformable-object manipulation methods address individual routing operations, but complete harness installation requires simultaneously handling deformation, discrete ordering, and contact uncertainty, which current approaches do not combine. See McKenna and Oyekan (2026), *A Perspective on Open Challenges in Deformable Object Manipulation*, arXiv:2602.22998.
solved_when: A robot system completes full harness installation — routing through clips and confined passages — while satisfying bend radius, twist, tension, connector orientation, and serviceability constraints, combining deformation handling, discrete clip ordering, and contact uncertainty.
why: It automates labor-intensive electronics and vehicle assembly, where cable harness installation remains a manual bottleneck.
key_works: McKenna and Oyekan (2026), *A Perspective on Open Challenges in Deformable Object Manipulation*, arXiv:2602.22998.

title: Cutting unknown heterogeneous materials
open: How can a robot adapt its cutting trajectory and applied forces in real time when the material it cuts contains hidden inclusions, anisotropy, or changing fracture behavior? Formally, the goal is an adaptive cutting strategy that achieves the desired cut shape and damage constraints despite unknown, heterogeneous material properties.
status: RoboNinja (Xu et al. (2023), *RoboNinja: Learning an Adaptive Cutting Policy for Multi-Material Objects*, arXiv:2302.11553) demonstrates adaptive cutting of multimaterial objects; extending to wider material classes and calibrated failure prediction remains open.
solved_when: A cutting system is demonstrated that adapts trajectories and forces to hidden inclusions, anisotropy, and changing fracture behavior while meeting the stated shape and damage constraints, across material classes beyond those already handled, together with calibrated prediction of failure.
why: It would enable reliable robotic cutting in food preparation, recycling, manufacturing, and surgery, where materials vary and cannot be characterized in advance.
key_works: Xu et al. (2023), *RoboNinja: Learning an Adaptive Cutting Policy for Multi-Material Objects*, arXiv:2302.11553.

title: Online rheology identification during manipulation
open: Can a robot infer a material's task-relevant viscoelastic, plastic, or granular properties while it is already manipulating that material, and adapt its control on the fly? In other words, can identification of history-dependent constitutive behavior be performed online, jointly with manipulation, rather than through a separate characterization experiment?
status: Current deformable-object control relies on learned or fitted models, and jointly identifying history-dependent constitutive behavior remains difficult. A survey of open challenges is Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767.
solved_when: A manipulation system demonstrates online identification of task-relevant viscoelastic, plastic, and granular properties during ongoing manipulation, with control adapting based on the identified properties and no separate characterization experiment required.
why: It would make materials that resist accurate pre-modeling — doughs, gels, biological tissue, soft packaging — tractable targets for robotic manipulation.
key_works: Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767.

title: Dynamic cloth manipulation with predictable landing states
open: Can a robot dynamically manipulate — fling, shake, or toss — an unfamiliar textile so that it lands in a specified fold or pose, rather than merely spreading it out? Formally, the goal is precise control of the cloth's final landing state within given tolerances, for fabrics not seen during training.
status: FlingBot demonstrates effective dynamic unfolding of cloth; precise final-state control across fabrics remains a stronger, unmet target. See Ha and Song (2022), *FlingBot: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Dynamic Manipulation for Cloth Unfolding*, arXiv:2105.03655.
solved_when: A demonstrated system achieves, across diverse unfamiliar fabrics, final folds and poses falling within pre-specified tolerances — not just increased visible coverage.
why: Reliable dynamic manipulation with predictable landing states would dramatically shorten laundry and fabric-handling cycles.
key_works: Ha and Song (2022), *FlingBot: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Dynamic Manipulation for Cloth Unfolding*, arXiv:2105.03655.

title: Cross-material deformable-manipulation benchmarks
open: Can we build deformable-object manipulation benchmarks that measure real material properties, provide hidden-state ground truth, record damage outcomes, and test generalization to held-out materials — rather than only reporting simulator-specific task success? Formally, the goal is a data infrastructure whose evaluation extends beyond a single simulation environment to cross-material physical transfer.
status: SoftGym (Lin et al. (2020), arXiv:2011.07215) supplies a useful simulation benchmark; physical cross-material transfer and standardized damage measurement still require additional infrastructure.
solved_when: A benchmark exists that includes measured material properties, hidden-state ground truth, damage outcomes, and held-out material evaluation, going beyond simulator-specific task success alone.
why: Such a benchmark reveals whether reported progress reflects transferable manipulation skill or merely exploitation of one simulator's quirks; without standardized damage measurement, cross-material claims cannot be validated physically.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), *SoftGym*, arXiv:2011.07215.

title: Sim-to-real transfer under unmodeled physics
open: When can a policy trained entirely in simulation be trusted to run on a real robot whose physics the simulator fails to capture—contact, latency, deformation, or sensing mechanisms absent from the model rather than merely different parameter values?
status: Domain randomization enabled dexterous transfer, as in OpenAI et al. (2018/2020), *Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation*, arXiv:1808.00177; however, expanding a parameter distribution cannot represent every structural model error.
solved_when: A theoretical characterization exists of the conditions under which sim-trained policies provably transfer to real systems containing structural mechanisms absent from the simulator, going beyond parameter-distribution coverage.
why: It would tell robotists when simulation-only training can be trusted and when it silently fails, replacing heuristics with a sound basis for deploying learned control.
key_works: OpenAI et al. (2018/2020), *Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation*, arXiv:1808.00177.

title: Cross-embodiment learning without destructive averaging
open: Can robots with different kinematics, sensors, action interfaces, and capabilities learn shared skills from pooled experience without destructive averaging erasing their embodiment-specific constraints? Formally: a learning procedure whose shared representations transfer across embodiments while provably preserving each embodiment's own feasible action structure.
status: Open. The Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2023), *Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models*, arXiv:2310.08864, demonstrates benefits from pooled robot data; universal action semantics and reliable transfer remain broader targets.
solved_when: A method exists that learns shared skills across heterogeneous embodiments — differing kinematics, sensors, action interfaces, and capabilities — and demonstrably preserves embodiment-specific constraints rather than averaging them away, with reliable transfer evaluated across embodiments.
why: It would let experience collected on one robot directly improve the policies of others, multiplying the effective data available to every machine in a fleet.
key_works: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2023), *Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models*, arXiv:2310.08864.

title: Tenfold less real-robot data for new tasks
open: Can a robot system learn a new manipulation task to the same held-out success rate as today's best pipelines while using at least 10× fewer real demonstrations and interventions? Formally, the target is matched held-out task success with a budget of real demonstrations and interventions reduced tenfold, counting unsuccessful collection attempts in the tally.
status: Generalist policies and efficient demonstration interfaces provide the current baselines, e.g. Octo Model Team et al. (2024), *Octo: An Open-Source Generalist Robot Policy*, arXiv:2405.12213, and Chi et al. (2024), *Universal Manipulation Interface*, arXiv:2402.10329. Any fair evaluation target must count all physical data and human assistance, including failed collection attempts.
solved_when: Held-out task success matches the baseline on a defined set of new tasks, while total real-robot data — demonstrations plus interventions, including unsuccessful collection attempts — is reduced by a factor of at least 10.
why: It makes adaptation to new tasks affordable outside well-resourced laboratories.
key_works: Octo Model Team et al. (2024), *Octo: An Open-Source Generalist Robot Policy*, arXiv:2405.12213; Chi et al. (2024), *Universal Manipulation Interface*, arXiv:2402.10329.

title: Offline robot learning with hidden confounding
open: Can a robot learn the true consequences of its actions from expert demonstrations alone, when the expert's choices depended on information — tactile cues, intentions, or environmental state — that was never recorded?
status: Large datasets such as Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID: A Large-Scale In-The-Wild Robot Manipulation Dataset*, arXiv:2403.12945 improve coverage, but observational trajectories alone do not automatically identify causal effects.
solved_when: A method exists that identifies valid causal action consequences from purely observational demonstration data under hidden confounding, yielding policies whose learned effects transfer when the robot itself selects actions; no quantitative budget (dataset size, sample count) is specified, so the criterion is correctness of the identified consequences rather than scale.
why: Without it, policies copy spurious correlations from the demonstrator's behavior that fail the moment the robot chooses different actions.
key_works: Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID: A Large-Scale In-The-Wild Robot Manipulation Dataset*, arXiv:2403.12945.

title: Autonomous learning without human resets
open: Can a robot acquire new skills entirely on its own, restoring usable training states itself rather than relying on a human to reset the environment? In other words, can learning be made autonomous even when training episodes end in dropped, misplaced, or damaged objects?
status: Many current learning setups separate task execution from reset, treating reset as an external service; reset-free operation instead changes exploration, safety, and data accounting. Related directions include continuing reinforcement learning and reversible exploration. Key work: Brunke et al. (2022), *Safe Learning in Robotics: From Learning-Based Control to Safe Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2108.06266.
