solved_when: A learning system demonstrates sustained skill acquisition in which the robot itself recovers from dropped, misplaced, or damaged objects and restores usable training states, with no human resets or intervention required during the learning process.
why: It removes a major hidden labor requirement from autonomous learning, making long-duration robot training practical without constant human supervision.
key_works: Brunke et al. (2022), *Safe Learning in Robotics: From Learning-Based Control to Safe Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2108.06266.

title: Active collection of the most valuable robot experience
open: Which demonstrations and autonomous trials should a robot collect next so as to maximize improvement in future deployment performance per unit of total cost, where cost couples together operator time, hardware wear, and failure risk?
status: Diverse datasets such as Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID*, arXiv:2403.12945, broaden the robot's experience base, but principled data acquisition under coupled physical costs remains a separate, open optimization problem.
solved_when: A principled acquisition rule is given that, given a budget accounting for operator time, wear, and failure risk, selects the next demonstration or trial so as to maximize deployment improvement per unit of total cost — with a formal account of the coupled-cost objective.
why: It directs expensive real-world experiments toward the failures that matter, rather than broad but undirected data collection.
key_works: Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID*, arXiv:2403.12945.

title: Representations invariant to irrelevant scene changes
open: Can we learn action representations that are invariant to background, lighting, and incidental objects, yet still sensitive to subtle task-relevant differences such as contact state or a latch position? Formally, the goal is a representation that discards provably irrelevant scene variation while preserving the distinctions that matter for control.
status: Visuomotor policies such as Chi et al. (2023), *Diffusion Policy*, arXiv:2303.04137 demonstrate broad practical gains; invariance and sensitivity must be balanced rather than maximized independently.
solved_when: A learned representation demonstrably ignores irrelevant scene changes (background, lighting, incidental objects) while retaining sensitivity to task-relevant differences like contact state or latch position, with invariance and sensitivity balanced rather than maximized independently.
why: It reduces brittle failures of visuomotor policies caused by visually unfamiliar but physically equivalent scenes.
key_works: Chi et al. (2023), *Diffusion Policy*, arXiv:2303.04137.

title: Grounding underspecified instructions in physical affordances
open: Can a robot take a vague instruction like “put this away safely” and work out what to do from the actual scene, the user’s constraints, and its own physical capabilities, asking the human only the clarifying questions it truly needs? Formally, this is a joint grounding problem: mapping an underspecified natural-language goal onto scene affordances and robot skills while minimizing unnecessary clarification requests.
status: SayCan grounds language in skill affordances, but ambiguous goals and unmodeled constraints still require richer grounding; the open gap is handling the full scene–constraint–capability interaction with minimal clarification. Key work: Ahn et al. (2022), *Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances*, arXiv:2204.01691.
solved_when: A system exists that resolves underspecified instructions using scene, user constraints, and robot capabilities, and asks only the necessary clarifying questions rather than none or many; success is demonstrated on goals beyond curated commands.
why: It would make natural-language control of robots genuinely useful for everyday, loosely specified requests instead of only pre-scripted commands.
key_works: Ahn et al. (2022), *Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances*, arXiv:2204.01691.

title: Calibrated confidence for vision–language–action policies
open: Can a vision–language–action policy predict, before acting, whether a proposed action sequence will succeed or cause harm when deployed under distribution shift — and can that prediction be calibrated against actual physical outcomes rather than model likelihoods?
status: OpenVLA (Kim et al. (2024), *OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model*, arXiv:2406.09246) provides an open generalist policy, but its generative likelihood is not itself a calibrated task-success probability. Related directions include selective prediction under distribution shift and calibrated sequence prediction.
solved_when: A method exists that predicts action-sequence success or harm under deployment shift with calibration measured on physical outcomes.
why: It enables justified abstention, timely requests for human assistance, and risk-sensitive execution on real robots.
key_works: Kim et al. (2024), *OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model*, arXiv:2406.09246.

title: Compositional transfer of physical skills
open: Can a robot execute a task that is a new combination of objects, relations, and skills it has already mastered, without ever seeing a demonstration of that combination? Formally, this asks for systematic compositional generalization: performance on unseen combinations should follow from competence on the components, not from coverage of the combination space.
status: RT-2 (Brohan et al. (2023), *RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control*, arXiv:2307.15818) transfers web-derived knowledge into robotic control; its systematic compositional generalization is stronger than success on selected novel instructions.
solved_when: A system demonstrates reliable execution of novel combinations of familiar objects, relations, and skills without demonstrations of each specific combination, with compositional generalization that holds systematically rather than only on selected novel instructions.
why: Without it, data requirements grow combinatorially with the number of task combinations; with it, a finite library of skills and relations covers an open-ended space of tasks.
key_works: Brohan et al. (2023), *RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control*, arXiv:2307.15818.

title: Progress recognition without visual reward shortcuts
open: Determine whether a task is genuinely progressing or complete when appearances can be misleading—for example, a closed drawer that still obstructs an object.
status: Language-conditioned spatial representations enable useful task specification, as in Huang et al. (2023), *VoxPoser: Composable 3D Value Maps for Robotic Manipulation with Language Models*, arXiv:2307.05973; however, physical completion verification remains an additional requirement.
solved_when: A system can correctly distinguish true task completion from superficially convincing but false completion states across manipulation tasks with misleading visual appearances, avoiding false success reports.
why: Prevents false success reports and repeated ineffective actions by grounding progress recognition in physical outcome rather than visual shortcuts.
key_works: Huang et al. (2023), *VoxPoser: Composable 3D Value Maps for Robotic Manipulation with Language Models*, arXiv:2307.05973.

title: Counterfactual physical reasoning before action
open: Can a robot reason counterfactually about physics — predicting what would happen under alternative actions — well enough to reject plans that look plausible but are physically invalid? Formally, this asks whether models can evaluate support, containment, force, and irreversibility consequences of candidate actions before executing them.
status: General robot control models demonstrate broad behavior, but reliable counterfactual reasoning is not established merely by producing fluent plans. Key work: Black et al. (2024/2025), *π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control*, arXiv:2410.24164.
solved_when: A model can, prior to execution, correctly reject physically invalid plans while accepting valid ones, where invalidity involves support, containment, force, or irreversible changes.
why: It reduces mistakes that cannot be repaired after execution.
key_works: Black et al. (2024/2025), *π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control*, arXiv:2410.24164.

title: Verifiable language-generated robot programs
open: Can a robot's language model turn a natural-language instruction into an executable control program that is verifiably safe — with checked preconditions, resource bounds, authority limits, and safe fallback behavior when perception is wrong? Formally, this asks for a pipeline in which generated programs carry explicit physical and authorization contracts that a verifier can check before execution.
status: Code as Policies (Liang et al. (2022), *Code as Policies: Language Model Programs for Embodied Control*, arXiv:2209.07753) demonstrates language-generated control code; full physical and authorization contracts require additional verification.
solved_when: An instruction-to-program system produces executable code together with machine-checkable guarantees covering precondition satisfaction, resource bounds, authority limits, and safe behavior under faulty perception, such that generated programs cannot bypass safety through valid-looking API calls.
why: It prevents generated programs from bypassing safety through valid-looking API calls, closing the gap between code that merely appears correct and code that is provably safe to run on a physical robot.
key_works: Liang et al. (2022), *Code as Policies: Language Model Programs for Embodied Control*, arXiv:2209.07753.

title: Reward synthesis that resists exploitation
open: Can we synthesize robot-training objectives that keep producing the intended behavior even when an optimizer pushes hard against them — including for costs left out of the demonstrations, such as damage, nuisance, and unsafe shortcuts?
status: Eureka — Ma et al. (2023), *Eureka: Human-Level Reward Design via Coding Large Language Models*, arXiv:2310.12931 — demonstrates effective automated reward design; however, optimization-resistant specification remains a stronger, unmet requirement. Related lines of thought include Goodhart's law and inverse reward design.
solved_when: A reward-synthesis method exists whose objectives preserve intended behavior under optimization, covering omitted costs like damage, nuisance, and unsafe shortcuts.
why: It prevents the training of policies that look impressive on the specified objective but are operationally unacceptable in deployment.
key_works: Ma et al. (2023), *Eureka: Human-Level Reward Design via Coding Large Language Models*, arXiv:2310.12931.

title: Long-horizon execution in genuinely unfamiliar homes
open: Can a robot reliably carry out extended household workflows — with mid-task recoveries, occupants and routines that change, and objects stored in unfamiliar places — in homes it has never seen before, without any per-home tuning? More formally, the question is whether long-horizon domestic execution can be achieved by generalist policies under distribution shift, with no per-environment adaptation or hand-engineered recovery logic.
status: π0.5 reports open-world generalization, including to unfamiliar homes, but sustained reliability and recovery remain beyond what a single successful generalization demonstration shows (Physical Intelligence et al. (2025), *π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization*, arXiv:2504.16054).
solved_when: A system completes extended household workflows in genuinely unfamiliar homes, handling recoveries and changing occupants and unfamiliar object organization, at sustained reliability — beyond a single successful generalization demonstration — with no per-home tuning.
why: It is the bridge between generalist-policy research and domestic autonomy that is actually useful; without sustained recovery in unseen homes, generalist demonstrations remain anecdotes rather than deployable capability.
key_works: Physical Intelligence et al. (2025), *π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization*, arXiv:2504.16054.

title: Weeks of useful work without unrecorded intervention
open: Can a robot perform genuinely useful work continuously for weeks while keeping a complete, honest record of every human intervention it receives? Concretely, can sustained operation be demonstrated with full logs of all repairs, resets, teleoperation, cleaning, charging assistance, and task exclusions?
status: Long-term autonomy has an established research history — see Kunze et al. (2018), *Artificial Intelligence for Long-Term Robot Autonomy: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.05196 — but transparent accounting of all supporting labor is essential to reaching this stronger target, and no such demonstration exists yet at this standard.
solved_when: A robot completes weeks of useful real-world operation with a complete public log of every unrecorded-intervention category — repairs, resets, teleoperation, cleaning, charging assistance, and task exclusions — showing what fraction of its operation, if any, relied on such support.
why: It separates genuine autonomy from a robot propped up by an invisible operations team, giving an honest measure of what the system actually does on its own.
key_works: Kunze et al. (2018), *Artificial Intelligence for Long-Term Robot Autonomy: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.05196.

title: Distinguishing hardware faults from environmental novelty
open: Can a long-lived autonomous robot determine, from its own operational evidence alone, whether declining performance stems from hardware wear, a sensor failure, a change in its surroundings, or an inadequate policy? More formally, is there a principled diagnostic procedure that separates these confounded causes of performance degradation without privileged access to ground truth?
status: Long-term autonomy is understood to require monitoring and adaptation, but confounding among these failure causes remains difficult to resolve. Kunze et al. (2018), *Artificial Intelligence for Long-Term Robot Autonomy: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.05196.
solved_when: A method exists that, using only operational evidence available to the robot, correctly distinguishes wear, sensor failure, environmental change, and policy inadequacy as causes of poor performance, with the appropriate response (repair, safe shutdown, or retraining) identified for each case.
why: Misdiagnosis leads to inappropriate repairs, unsafe continued operation, or unnecessary retraining; a correct diagnosis routes the robot to the right recovery action.
key_works: Kunze et al. (2018), *Artificial Intelligence for Long-Term Robot Autonomy: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.05196.

title: Safe adaptation to previously unseen damage
open: How can a robot recover useful behavior after damage it was never designed or trained to anticipate, without exploratory actions that could worsen the damage or endanger nearby people? Formally, this asks for adaptation algorithms that achieve rapid performance recovery under strict safety constraints on every action taken during exploration.
status: Intelligent trial-and-error adaptation has demonstrated rapid recovery from selected damage cases (Cully et al. (2015), *Robots that can adapt like animals*, DOI:10.1038/nature14422; arXiv:1407.3501); unforeseen damage under strict safety constraints remains a broader, open target.
solved_when: An adaptation method demonstrably restores useful behavior after unanticipated damage while guaranteeing that no exploratory action worsens the damage or endangers people, on damage cases broader than the selected scenarios used in prior demonstrations.
why: It keeps remote or expensive robots useful after partial failures, where replacement or human intervention is impractical.
key_works: Cully et al. (2015), *Robots that can adapt like animals*, DOI:10.1038/nature14422; arXiv:1407.3501.

title: Self-recalibration after mechanical drift
open: Can a robot detect and correct changes in its own joint offsets, compliance, sensor alignment, and actuation as they arise during operation, without external metrology equipment or deliberately dangerous calibration motions?
status: Rapid adaptation methods, such as Kumar et al. (2021), *RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation for Legged Robots*, arXiv:2107.04034, infer latent dynamics during operation; however, full geometric and sensing recalibration requires additional observability beyond what these methods provide.
solved_when: A method exists that identifies drift in joint offsets, compliance, sensor alignment, and actuation from normal operation alone, with no external metrology and no dangerous calibration motions.
why: It preserves accuracy as robots age or receive replacement parts, avoiding the cost and downtime of external recalibration.
key_works: Kumar et al. (2021), *RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation for Legged Robots*, arXiv:2107.04034.

title: Autonomous physical self-repair
open: Can a robot autonomously repair its own hardware — diagnosing a replaceable fault, obtaining or manipulating a spare component, performing the replacement, and verifying restored capability — without another robot or a human doing the difficult steps?
status: The current state of the art is damage adaptation — robots that change their behavior to compensate for injury rather than repairing the physical hardware, as in Cully et al. (2015), *Robots that can adapt like animals*, DOI:10.1038/nature14422. This target goes further by adding physical restoration and verification of repaired capability.
solved_when: A single robot, unaided, completes the full pipeline: fault diagnosis, spare-part acquisition or manipulation, physical replacement, and verification that capability is restored.
why: Success would fundamentally change the economics of remote operation, where today a hardware fault typically ends the mission or demands human intervention.
key_works: Cully et al. (2015), *Robots that can adapt like animals*, DOI:10.1038/nature14422.

title: Joint scheduling of work, charging, and degradation
open: How should a robot jointly schedule its missions and charging when future demand is uncertain, its battery ages, thermal limits bind, and it may find itself unable to reach a charger at all? Formally, this asks for a scheduling policy that maximizes long-term productivity under uncertain demand, battery degradation, thermal constraints, and charger-reachability risk.
status: Energy management is established as part of long-term autonomy, and degradation-aware operation is recognized as adding a long-horizon resource tradeoff, but no solution to the joint problem is recorded. Kunze et al. (2018), *Artificial Intelligence for Long-Term Robot Autonomy: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.05196.
solved_when: A scheduling policy exists that jointly handles work, charging, battery aging, thermal limits, and charger-reachability risk under uncertain future demand, with a provable or empirically demonstrated improvement in long-horizon productivity.
why: It improves a robot's lifetime productivity rather than only today's task count, turning degradation-aware operation into a manageable long-horizon resource tradeoff.
key_works: Kunze et al. (2018), *Artificial Intelligence for Long-Term Robot Autonomy: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.05196.

title: Useful autonomy through cloud and network outages
open: Can a robot keep executing its tasks safely and coherently when the remote services it depends on — cloud inference, shared maps, identity services, or fleet coordination — become unavailable? In formal terms, the goal is an autonomy architecture that maintains safe, coherent task execution under partial or total loss of remote connectivity.
status: ROS 2 supports distributed robotic systems, but application-level continuity across partial service failures remains a separate responsibility of the system designer; no framework-level guarantee exists. Key reference: Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2: Design, Architecture, and Uses In The Wild*, arXiv:2211.07752.
solved_when: A robotic system is demonstrated to preserve safe, coherent task execution through outages of remote inference, maps, identity services, or fleet coordination, with application-level continuity across partial service failures handled explicitly rather than assumed away.
why: It prevents network availability from becoming a hidden safety assumption — a robot whose safety silently depends on connectivity is unsafe precisely when conditions are worst.
key_works: Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2: Design, Architecture, and Uses In The Wild*, arXiv:2211.07752.

title: Restart recovery without duplicate physical actions
open: After a controller restart, how can a robot determine which of its actions physically took place before the interruption, so that it can resume without repeating an irreversible action? Formally, the goal is a recovery procedure that reconstructs the set of completed physical effects (dispensing, cutting, fastening, object transfer) from available state despite those effects being unobserved at the moment of the restart.
status: Formal robotic verification addresses system behavior — see Luckcuck et al. (2019), *Formal Specification and Verification of Autonomous Robotic Systems: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.00048 — but durable software state alone cannot reveal an unobserved physical effect, and no existing method closes this gap.
solved_when: A restart-recovery method exists that correctly determines which physical actions already occurred and resumes execution without any duplicate dispensing, cutting, fastening, or object transfer.
why: It makes retrying after a crash safe for actions that cannot be undone, so a restart can never cause a robot to double-dispense, double-cut, or double-transfer in the physical world.
key_works: Luckcuck et al. (2019), *Formal Specification and Verification of Autonomous Robotic Systems: A Survey*, arXiv:1807.00048.

title: End-to-end safety contracts that include perception
open: Can we prove useful end-to-end safety properties for a robotic system whose controller's state estimate comes from fallible learned perception, rather than assuming exact state or a fixed bounded error? Formally stated: establish safety guarantees that account for the perception module itself, not only for the controller conditioned on trusted state information.
status: Current safe-learning methods provide only conditional guarantees, and perception failures can violate the very conditions on which those guarantees depend. Key works: Brunke et al. (2022), *Safe Learning in Robotics*, arXiv:2108.06266.
solved_when: A proof framework yields useful safety guarantees for a closed-loop system whose state estimate is produced by learned perception, without assuming exact state or a pre-specified bounded perception error, and the guarantees remain valid when perception errs.
why: It closes a major gap between controller-level proofs and deployed robotic systems, where state is never exact and perception can fail in unmodeled ways.
key_works: Brunke et al. (2022), *Safe Learning in Robotics*, arXiv:2108.06266.

title: High-dimensional reachability without unsafe approximation
open: Can we compute useful reachable sets for high-dimensional robot dynamics while controlling approximation error and meeting real-time requirements?
status: Hamilton–Jacobi reachability gives strong guarantees for tractable state dimensions, but dimensional scaling remains a central obstacle; see Bansal et al. (2017), *Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability: A Brief Overview and Recent Advances*, arXiv:1709.07523.
solved_when: An algorithm computes reachable sets for high-dimensional dynamics with controlled approximation error and computation fast enough for real-time use.
why: It enables principled collision avoidance and recoverability analysis for systems where exact methods are intractable.
key_works: Bansal et al. (2017), *Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability: A Brief Overview and Recent Advances*, arXiv:1709.07523.

title: Closed-loop conformal guarantees under adaptive distribution shift
open: Can we obtain meaningful finite-sample risk guarantees for a robot whose own actions change the distribution of the data it observes? Formally, the question is how conformal-style guarantees survive when closed-loop deployment breaks the exchangeability assumptions on which they rest.
status: Conformal methods are being integrated with formal verification and control; adaptive closed-loop deployment currently requires additional assumptions or new theory. Key work: Lindemann et al. (2024), *Formal Verification and Control with Conformal Prediction*, arXiv:2409.00536.
solved_when: A framework is provided that retains finite-sample risk guarantees under adaptive distribution shift caused by the agent's own actions, with rigorously stated assumptions replacing exchangeability.
why: It would make statistical safety claims valid for systems that act on the world, not just passively observe it — the setting in which conformal methods are actually deployed.
key_works: Lindemann et al. (2024), *Formal Verification and Control with Conformal Prediction*, arXiv:2409.00536.

title: Barrier functions across contact-mode transitions
open: Can we construct control barrier functions that guarantee safety across the full set of contact-mode transitions in hybrid systems — through impact, sticking, sliding, and contact loss — even when the times of those transitions are uncertain? Formally, this asks for a barrier-function framework whose validity is preserved at mode switches without assuming known switching times.
status: Barrier-function theory provides powerful tools for continuous systems, but hybrid contact dynamics require additional compatibility conditions that current theory does not supply; hybrid invariance and viability theory are related lines of work. Reference: Ames et al. (2019), *Control Barrier Functions: Theory and Applications*, arXiv:1903.11199.
solved_when: A construction of control barrier functions is given that remains valid through impact, sticking, sliding, and contact loss, and whose safety guarantee holds despite uncertain transition times.
why: It would extend safety filtering — now mature for continuous dynamics — to dexterous and legged robot behavior, where contact-mode changes are unavoidable.
key_works: Ames et al. (2019), *Control Barrier Functions: Theory and Applications*, arXiv:1903.11199.

title: Safe exploration when the safe set is initially unknown
open: How much can an agent learn about its environment while remaining safe, when the very notion of safety must itself be inferred from experience rather than specified in advance? Formally, the problem asks for a characterization of what is learnable under safety constraints that are initially unknown.
status: Safe reinforcement learning typically needs initial safe knowledge, conservative models, or recoverable regions; the necessity of these assumptions deserves sharper bounds. See Brunke et al. (2022), *Safe Learning in Robotics*, arXiv:2108.06266.
solved_when: A characterization is given — impossibility results and/or achievable-learning bounds — showing which guarantees are attainifiable without initial safe knowledge, conservative models, or recoverable regions, with sharp bounds on when these assumptions are necessary.
why: It separates the autonomous learning that is actually achievable from the safety guarantees that are impossible without prior knowledge, telling us which assumptions safe learning systems genuinely require.
key_works: Brunke et al. (2022), *Safe Learning in Robotics*, arXiv:2108.06266.

title: Verification of large learned policies in closed loop
open: Can we formally verify a robot's complete learned stack — perception, policy, and dynamics composed together — over meaningful time horizons and operational regions, without collapsing the specification into a trivially checkable local property?
status: Formal methods today verify restricted robotic components and systems; large neural and hybrid compositions create state-space and modeling barriers. A survey of the area is Luckcuck et al. (2019), *Formal Specification and Verification of Autonomous Robotic Systems*, arXiv:1807.00048. Related directions include neural-network verification and compositional model checking.
solved_when: A verification method exists that covers the full perception–policy–dynamics composition in closed loop over nontrivial time horizons and operational regions, with the verified specification retaining the intended safety property rather than a weakened local surrogate.
why: It produces evidence of correctness stronger than passing a finite collection of test scenarios, which is the current de facto standard for deploying learned robotic systems.
key_works: Luckcuck et al. (2019), *Formal Specification and Verification of Autonomous Robotic Systems*, arXiv:1807.00048.

title: Composing risk across long missions
open: How should a robot allocate and update a mission-wide risk budget when failures are dependent, exposure changes over time, and task selection adapts to observations?
status: Per-action or per-trajectory guarantees do not automatically provide informative lifetime guarantees; the state of the art is represented by Lindemann et al. (2024), *Formal Verification and Control with Conformal Prediction*, arXiv:2409.00536.
solved_when: A method exists that converts per-action or per-trajectory safety guarantees into informative lifetime (mission-wide) risk guarantees under dependent failures, time-varying exposure, and adaptive task selection.
why: Without such composition, individually "safe" actions can accumulate unacceptable operational risk over a long mission.
key_works: Lindemann et al. (2024), *Formal Verification and Control with Conformal Prediction*, arXiv:2409.00536.

title: Locomotion over visually deceptive terrain
open: How can a legged robot cross terrain whose visual appearance misrepresents its mechanical support — vegetation concealing holes, thin crusts, loose coverings, transparent obstacles? The goal is a locomotion capability that reasons about hidden load-bearing and traction properties not recoverable from images alone.
status: Perceptive locomotion systems demonstrate impressive outdoor robustness, but hidden load-bearing properties remain a distinct uncertainty; see Miki et al. (2022), *Learning robust perceptive locomotion for quadrupedal robots in the wild*, arXiv:2201.08117.
solved_when: A locomotion system demonstrates traversal of surfaces whose appearance misrepresents support or traction — such as vegetation over holes, thin crusts, loose coverings, and transparent obstacles — rather than only terrain recognizable from visual data.
why: It extends legged mobility beyond terrain whose properties can be inferred from images alone, addressing the gap where appearance and support disagree.
key_works: Miki et al. (2022), *Learning robust perceptive locomotion for quadrupedal robots in the wild*, arXiv:2201.08117.

title: Foothold selection with uncertain friction and compliance
open: Can a legged robot choose where and how to step when it does not yet know whether a surface will hold — selecting footholds and contact forces while simultaneously estimating each contact's friction, compliance, and risk of failure? Formally, the problem is to jointly plan contacts and identify, prospectively, the stability properties of surfaces never tested under load.
status: Rapid adaptation (e.g., Kumar et al. (2021), *RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation for Legged Robots*, arXiv:2107.04034) handles changing dynamics, but anticipating a previously untested foothold adds a prospective identification problem that current methods do not address. Related framings include dual control and chance-constrained contact planning.
solved_when: A method exists that selects footholds and contact forces together with an estimate of whether each candidate surface will slip, deform, or collapse, in a way that anticipates untested footholds rather than reacting after contact.
why: It reduces falls before the controller has accumulated enough evidence to adapt, closing the gap between rapid reactive adaptation and prospective safety on unknown terrain.
key_works: Kumar et al. (2021), *RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation for Legged Robots*, arXiv:2107.04034.

title: Controlled falling and recovery in clutter
open: Can a legged robot, once a fall becomes unavoidable, choose a fall trajectory that minimizes injury and damage, and then recover to operation from an arbitrary reachable resting configuration — without assuming clear surrounding space?
status: Agile locomotion has advanced substantially, but ordinary locomotion benchmarks do not establish safe failure and recovery behavior. Related directions include impact optimization and recoverability in hybrid systems; see Zhuang, Yao, and Zhao (2025), *Humanoid Parkour Learning*, PMLR 270:1975–1991.
solved_when: A system demonstrably selects damage-minimizing fall trajectories and recovers from arbitrary reachable resting configurations in cluttered environments, with no requirement of free space around the robot.
why: It makes inevitable failures survivable in occupied environments, where people and obstacles are present rather than cleared away.
key_works: Zhuang, Yao, and Zhao (2025), *Humanoid Parkour Learning*, PMLR 270:1975–1991.

title: Whole-body locomotion while manipulating uncertain loads
open: How can a legged robot coordinate stepping, balance, arm motion, and contact forces when the mass or contents of the object it carries change unexpectedly? Formally, the goal is a whole-body locomotion-and-manipulation controller that remains stable and effective under sudden, unmodeled changes in load properties.
status: Whole-body mobile manipulation and agile locomotion each have separate strong demonstrations — e.g., Fu et al. (2024), *Mobile ALOHA*, arXiv:2401.02117, and Zhuang et al. (2025), *Humanoid Parkour Learning* — but their robust integration remains demanding.
solved_when: A controller achieves coordinated stepping, balance, arm motion, and contact-force management on hardware while carrying loads whose mass or contents change without warning, maintaining stability and manipulation performance throughout — not merely in locomotion-only or manipulation-only settings.
why: Robust integration of these capabilities enables useful carrying and tool work, moving beyond demonstrations that showcase locomotion or manipulation in isolation.
key_works: Fu et al. (2024), *Mobile ALOHA*, arXiv:2401.02117; Zhuang et al. (2025), *Humanoid Parkour Learning*.

title: Agile locomotion with meaningful human-safety envelopes
open: Can a legged robot keep its speed and agility while provably respecting impact, separation, and emergency-stop requirements around people whose behavior cannot be predicted? In other words, can human-safety envelopes be made a first-class constraint of agile locomotion rather than a brake on it?
status: Parkour policies demonstrate complex traversal, but human-compatible safety is a different objective from obstacle-course completion. Rudin et al. (2026), *Parkour in the wild: Learning a general and extensible agile locomotion policy using multi-expert distillation and RL fine-tuning*, DOI:10.1177/02783649261455067.
solved_when: A locomotion system demonstrates useful speed and agility while enforcing impact, separation, and emergency-stop requirements around unpredictable humans, rather than merely completing obstacle courses.
why: This determines whether agile robots can operate in ordinary shared human spaces rather than only controlled environments.
key_works: Rudin et al. (2026), *Parkour in the wild: Learning a general and extensible agile locomotion policy using multi-expert distillation and RL fine-tuning*, DOI:10.1177/02783649261455067.

title: Thermally sustainable locomotion policies
open: Can a legged robot learn a locomotion policy that sustains useful work over long durations by reasoning about motor, gearbox, battery, and electronics temperatures, rather than merely respecting instantaneous torque limits? Formally, the goal is a gait-optimization formulation whose constraints and objectives capture thermal accumulation across the full actuation and power chain.
status: Rapidly trained locomotion policies, in the style of Rudin et al. (2021), *Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning* (arXiv:2109.11978), demonstrate strong motor skills, but thermal accumulation demands longer-horizon objectives and thermal models that current training pipelines do not include. Related directions include electrothermal co-optimization and constrained optimal control.
solved_when: A trained policy completes long-duration useful work while keeping motor, gearbox, battery, and electronics temperatures within their thermal limits, instead of only satisfying instantaneous torque constraints; success should be demonstrated over horizons long enough that thermal accumulation, not instantaneous limits, is the binding factor.
why: Without thermal awareness, short demonstrations mask unsustainable duty cycles — a policy that looks impressive in minutes may overheat actuators, batteries, or electronics during real long-duration deployment.
key_works: Rudin et al. (2021), *Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2109.11978.

title: Locomotion transfer across substantial morphology changes
open: Can a robot trained to walk retain its gait competence when its body changes substantially — different leg lengths, mass distributions, joint arrangements, or actuator capabilities — without extensive retraining? Formally, is there a transfer framework that preserves locomotion ability across morphology changes that alter controllability and feasible contact patterns, rather than merely shifting parameters?
status: Adaptation and domain randomization handle important variations, as in Kumar et al. (2021), *RMA*, arXiv:2107.04034 and Rudin et al. (2021), *Learning to Walk in Minutes*, arXiv:2109.11978; however, changes in controllability and feasible contact patterns require more than parameter tuning.
solved_when: A policy or representation is demonstrated that transfers walking competence across changes in leg lengths, mass distributions, joint arrangements, and actuator capabilities without extensive retraining.
why: It would sharply reduce the training cost of each new robot design, so hardware iteration would no longer require relearning locomotion from scratch.
key_works: Kumar et al. (2021), *RMA*, arXiv:2107.04034; Rudin et al. (2021), *Learning to Walk in Minutes*, arXiv:2109.11978.

title: Field measurements of gait-induced wear
open: How do the gaits a locomotion policy actually uses shape the long-term wear of a legged robot — its joints, feet, and fasteners — and the maintenance intervals these demand, under real terrain and weather rather than lab conditions?
status: Outdoor and energy-efficient locomotion demonstrations exist and provide baselines, e.g. Badri-Spröwitz et al. (2022), *BirdBot achieves energy-efficient gait with minimal control using avian-inspired leg clutching*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abg4055; however, standardized longitudinal wear comparisons remain a separate, unmet experimental target.
solved_when: A longitudinal field study produces standardized, comparable wear measurements across locomotion policies, quantifying effects on joint wear, foot degradation, fastener loosening, and maintenance intervals in real outdoor terrain and weather.
why: It would let designers optimize robot lifetime and service cost rather than only speed or benchmark success, which current demonstrations do not capture.
key_works: Badri-Spröwitz et al. (2022), *BirdBot achieves energy-efficient gait with minimal control using avian-inspired leg clutching*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abg4055.

title: High-speed flight under unfamiliar gusts and visibility
open: Can a drone flying at high speed keep avoiding collisions when the world around it stops matching its training data — gusts it has never felt, lighting it has never seen, rain, and aerodynamic disturbances beyond the nominal envelope?
status: High-speed flight in the wild and champion-level drone racing have both been demonstrated, but those achievements do not establish universal robustness to unfamiliar disturbances. Key works: Loquercio et al. (2021), *Learning High-Speed Flight in the Wild*, arXiv:2110.05113; Kaufmann et al. (2023), *Champion-level drone racing using deep reinforcement learning*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06419-4.
solved_when: A flight system demonstrates collision avoidance at high speed under gusts, lighting, precipitation, and aerodynamic disturbances that depart from its training conditions, with robustness to unfamiliar disturbances rather than only those seen in training.
why: It would make drone inspection and emergency response reliable outside prepared courses, where weather and wind cannot be scripted in advance.
key_works: Loquercio et al. (2021), *Learning High-Speed Flight in the Wild*, arXiv:2110.05113; Kaufmann et al. (2023), *Champion-level drone racing using deep reinforcement learning*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06419-4.

title: Fully onboard grasping of unfamiliar moving targets
open: Can a flying robot grasp an object it has never seen before while that object is moving, using only its own onboard sensing and computation? Formally: achieve grasping of dynamically moving targets with unknown geometry and unknown motion, without motion capture or prior object models.
status: Ubellacker et al. (2024), *High-speed aerial grasping using a soft drone with onboard perception*, DOI:10.1038/s44182-024-00012-1, demonstrated onboard grasping of static targets at speeds up to 2 m/s; their moving-target experiments relied on motion capture.
solved_when: A system demonstrates grasping of moving targets with unknown geometry and motion entirely onboard — no motion capture, no prior object models — with quantitative performance at least matching the 2 m/s speed regime of prior static-target onboard work.
why: It unlocks dynamic pickup, emergency supply transfer, and aerial logistics, where targets cannot be assumed stationary or instrumented.
key_works: Ubellacker et al. (2024), *High-speed aerial grasping using a soft drone with onboard perception*, DOI:10.1038/s44182-024-00012-1.

title: Rapid identification of payload-induced aerodynamics
open: How can a flying robot, in the moments right after grasping an unfamiliar payload, quickly estimate the new drag, downwash blockage, inertia, and center of mass it has just acquired — and compensate for them in flight?
status: Current adaptive aerial grasping methods compensate for added mass, but broad payload geometry introduces additional coupled aerodynamic effects that remain unaddressed. Key work: Ubellacker et al. (2024), *High-speed aerial grasping using a soft drone with onboard perception*, DOI:10.1038/s44182-024-00012-1.
solved_when: A system demonstrates stable, controlled flight immediately after grasping an arbitrary payload, with online estimation and compensation of the payload-induced changes in inertia, drag, downwash blockage, and center of mass.
why: Without rapid identification, a mechanically successful grasp destabilizes the vehicle — turning a completed manipulation task into a crash.
key_works: Ubellacker et al. (2024), *High-speed aerial grasping using a soft drone with onboard perception*, DOI:10.1038/s44182-024-00012-1.

title: Stable aerial force application on uncertain surfaces
open: How can a flying robot press on a surface with a controlled, stable force while simultaneously maintaining stable flight? Concretely, this asks for control of aerial contact tasks such as drilling, wiping, inspection, or fastening that maintains prescribed contact forces despite wind, surface compliance, and uncertain reaction forces.
status: Aerial manipulation prototypes demonstrate contact tasks, but outdoor robustness and the coupling between force application and flight control remain challenging; see Barakou, Tzafestas, and Valavanis (2024), *A Review of Real-Time Implementable Cooperative Aerial Manipulation Systems*, DOI:10.3390/drones8050196.
solved_when: An aerial manipulator demonstrates maintenance of prescribed contact forces during a contact task under wind, unknown surface compliance, and uncertain reaction forces, with robustness shown outdoors rather than only in laboratory conditions.
why: It would let flying robots actively perform maintenance — drilling, wiping, inspecting, fastening — instead of only observing, and the coupled force–flight control needed is exactly what current prototypes lack.
key_works: Barakou, Tzafestas, and Valavanis (2024), *A Review of Real-Time Implementable Cooperative Aerial Manipulation Systems*, DOI:10.3390/drones8050196.

title: Cooperative aerial transport with delayed communication
open: Can a team of aircraft jointly transport and precisely place a load that no single one could carry, while tolerating communication delays, cable slack, wind, and the failure of one aircraft? Formally, the goal is a cooperative aerial transport system that maintains load control and placement accuracy under delayed communication and these disturbances.
status: Cooperative aerial manipulation has laboratory demonstrations; the review by Barakou et al. (2024), *A Review of Real-Time Implementable Cooperative Aerial Manipulation Systems*, DOI:10.3390/drones8050196, identifies outdoor disturbances and communication as continuing difficulties.
solved_when: A multi-aircraft system transports and precisely places a shared load in the presence of communication delays, cable slack, wind, and a single-aircraft failure.
why: It enables transport of objects beyond one aircraft's capacity, such as heavy or bulky loads in outdoor environments.
key_works: Barakou et al. (2024), *A Review of Real-Time Implementable Cooperative Aerial Manipulation Systems*, DOI:10.3390/drones8050196.

title: Reliable perching and departure across surface classes
open: Can a flying robot approach, attach to, remain on, and later depart from an unfamiliar surface — whether natural or engineered — using a single attachment mechanism that is not tailored to that surface class? Formally, the goal is a perching and departure system that works reliably across diverse surface materials and geometries without surface-specific design.
status: Existing attachment approaches — spines, adhesives, and grippers — each handle only subsets of surfaces, and versatile attachment remains limited by dependence on surface material and geometry. A survey, *Current Status, Challenges, and Prospects for New Types of Aerial Robots* (2024), DOI:10.1016/j.eng.2024.05.008, documents this state of the art (author list **(verify)**).
solved_when: A single mechanism is demonstrated to approach, attach to, perch on, and depart from both natural and engineered surfaces without surface-specific attachment hardware, with performance no longer materially limited by the surface's material or geometry.
why: Perching extends flight endurance and enables persistent observation from fixed vantage points, capabilities currently out of reach for aerial robots that must stay airborne.
key_works: *Current Status, Challenges, and Prospects for New Types of Aerial Robots* (2024), DOI:10.1016/j.eng.2024.05.008; author list **(verify)**.

title: Insect-scale untethered flight with useful autonomy
open: Can a robot the weight and size of an insect fly, sense, decide, and communicate entirely on board — no tether, no external power, no motion-capture support — while doing a useful task? Formally, the challenge is to integrate propulsion, energy, sensing, control, and communication on a single insect-scale aircraft capable of untethered autonomous operation.
status: Flapping-wing and miniature aerial systems continue to advance the individual components, but integrated endurance and autonomy remain a coupled scaling problem. See *Current Status, Challenges, and Prospects for New Types of Aerial Robots* (2024), DOI:10.1016/j.eng.2024.05.008; author list **(verify)**.
solved_when: A single insect-scale aircraft integrating propulsion, energy, sensing, control, and communication demonstrates a useful task without external power or external state tracking.
why: It opens access to confined spaces inaccessible to larger robots and enables distributed environmental sensing at scale.
key_works: *Current Status, Challenges, and Prospects for New Types of Aerial Robots* (2024), DOI:10.1016/j.eng.2024.05.008; author list **(verify)**.

title: Emergency landing after partial actuator failure
open: Can an autonomous aircraft, having suffered a partial actuator or sensing failure, find and execute a landing maneuver that keeps people on the ground safe even when terrain is uncertain? More formally: compute an emergency landing strategy under post-failure dynamics that trades off survivability, terrain uncertainty, and risk to nearby people.
status: Agile flight research provides sophisticated nominal control, exemplified by Kaufmann et al. (2023), *Champion-level drone racing using deep reinforcement learning*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06419-4; failure recovery, however, requires different dynamics, objectives, and validation. Related directions include fault-tolerant flight control and minimum-risk reachable sets.
solved_when: A landing strategy exists that, after propulsion or sensing failure and under uncertain terrain with nearby people, is demonstrably survivable — validated against the different dynamics and objectives that failure induces, rather than nominal flight conditions.
why: It determines whether aerial autonomy can fail safely: without it, even champion-level nominal control cannot guarantee safe outcomes the moment hardware degrades.
key_works: Kaufmann et al. (2023), *Champion-level drone racing using deep reinforcement learning*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06419-4.

title: Continuous-time multi-agent pathfinding with physical dynamics
open: Can coordinated planning for many robots be scaled to settings where agents differ in shape, acceleration, and turning constraints, and where execution times are uncertain, rather than all moving in identical discrete grid steps? In other words, is there a formulation and algorithm for kinodynamic multi-agent pathfinding that retains tractability under heterogeneous physical dynamics and continuous time?
status: MAPF has clear discrete formulations and benchmarks, as established in Stern et al. (2019), *Multi-Agent Pathfinding: Definitions, Variants, and Benchmarks*, arXiv:1906.08291; realistic dynamics change both feasibility and the computational structure of the problem, and no equivalent formulation or benchmark exists for the kinodynamic setting.
solved_when: A planning formulation and algorithm exists that handles heterogeneous shapes, acceleration and turning constraints, and uncertain execution times at scale, with demonstrated tractability comparable to what discrete MAPF benchmarks achieve for identical grid agents.
why: It bridges algorithmic progress in MAPF to actual fleets, where physical dynamics — not grid abstraction — determine what plans are executable.
key_works: Stern et al. (2019), *Multi-Agent Pathfinding: Definitions, Variants, and Benchmarks*, arXiv:1906.08291.

title: Online fleet planning without starvation or gridlock
open: Can a fleet of robots be planned online — under continuous task arrivals, robot failures, blocked routes, and shifting priorities — so that progress is always guaranteed and no job is unfairly delayed? Formally, is there a planning policy for lifelong, disruption-prone multi-robot task allocation that simultaneously ensures system-wide progress and a bounded unfairness measure?
status: MAPF variants formalize many fleet-planning choices, as surveyed in Stern et al. (2019), *Multi-Agent Pathfinding*, arXiv:1906.08291; however, lifelong arrival and disruption models still require additional guarantees of the kind this problem targets.
solved_when: A policy exists that handles continuous task arrivals, failed robots, blocked routes, and changing priorities while providing provable progress guarantees and a bounded unfairness bound; alternatively, a negative result showing no such joint guarantee is achievable under these conditions.
why: Without such guarantees, efficient average throughput can indefinitely hide delayed jobs, starving individual tasks while aggregate metrics look healthy.
key_works: Stern et al. (2019), *Multi-Agent Pathfinding*, arXiv:1906.08291.

title: Heterogeneous task allocation with uncertain capabilities
open: How should a fleet of heterogeneous robots allocate cooperative tasks when each robot's skills, health, and availability — and the tasks' own requirements — are uncertain and change while the tasks are being executed?
status: Swarm engineering addresses coordination, but heterogeneous capability learning and allocation are more demanding than homogeneous role assignment; no method meeting the above criterion is known. Key reference: Brambilla et al. (2013), *Swarm robotics: a review from the swarm engineering perspective*, DOI:10.1007/s11721-012-0075-2.
solved_when: An allocation method exists that provably assigns cooperative tasks under evolving uncertainty in capabilities, health, availability, and task requirements during execution.
why: A solution makes mixed robot fleets resilient to degradation and failure, which is what makes them economically useful rather than fragile demonstrations.
key_works: Brambilla et al. (2013), *Swarm robotics: a review from the swarm engineering perspective*, DOI:10.1007/s11721-012-0075-2.

title: Synthesizing local rules with global guarantees
open: Can a swarm's desired collective behavior be compiled automatically into local rules for individual robots, so that convergence, robustness, and resource consumption are guaranteed rather than observed after the fact?
status: Swarms can exhibit useful collective behavior, but predictable engineering from specification remains a foundational challenge; see Brambilla et al. (2013), *Swarm robotics*, DOI:10.1007/s11721-012-0075-2, and Dorigo, Théraulaz, and Trianni (2020), *Reflections on the future of swarm robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abe4385.
solved_when: A method exists that, given a specification of a collective behavior, produces decentralized local rules with provable guarantees on convergence to that behavior, robustness to disturbances or failures, and bounds on resource consumption.
why: It would replace trial-and-error reliance on emergent dynamics with systematic, predictable swarm engineering.
key_works: Brambilla et al. (2013), *Swarm robotics*, DOI:10.1007/s11721-012-0075-2; Dorigo, Théraulaz, and Trianni (2020), *Reflections on the future of swarm robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abe4385.

title: Byzantine-resilient physical swarms
open: Can a physical swarm preserve its specified collective functions when some robots deliberately provide false information or act inconsistently, without relying on a trusted central controller? More formally, characterize what resilience is achievable against strategically Byzantine members in a decentralized robot swarm.
status: Robustness of swarms to ordinary failures does not automatically imply resilience to strategically misleading participants; no such characterization or construction is known. Dorigo et al. (2020), *Reflections on the future of swarm robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abe4385. Related directions include Byzantine agreement and adversarial distributed estimation.
solved_when: A characterization (or construction with proof) exists of swarm collective functions that can be maintained under a stated fraction of Byzantine robots, with no trusted central controller.
why: It protects infrastructure-scale fleets against compromised or malfunctioning members; robustness to ordinary failures alone does not confer resilience to strategic adversaries.
key_works: Dorigo et al. (2020), *Reflections on the future of swarm robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abe4385.

title: Communication lower bounds for embodied coordination
open: How much information must robots actually exchange to accomplish a given collective task when sensing is limited, occlusions and mobility interrupt visibility, and connectivity is intermittent? More precisely, what are tight, task-dependent lower bounds on the communication required for specified multi-robot coordination problems?
status: Local-rule swarms demonstrate coordination without rich communication; tight task-dependent lower bounds remain a distinct theoretical target. Key works: Brambilla et al. (2013), *Swarm robotics*, DOI:10.1007/s11721-012-0075-2.
solved_when: For specified collective tasks, tight communication lower bounds are established that account for limited sensing, occlusion, mobility, and intermittent connectivity — matching achievable upper bounds demonstrated by local-rule swarms.
why: Such bounds directly guide the design of radio, sensing, and control architectures, telling engineers when minimal communication suffices and when richer channels are unavoidable.
key_works: Brambilla et al. (2013), *Swarm robotics*, DOI:10.1007/s11721-012-0075-2.

title: Three-dimensional self-assembly with load-bearing guarantees
open: Can a swarm of mobile modules assemble and repair three-dimensional structures while every intermediate configuration remains mechanically stable? That is, can self-assembly proceed so that partial structures are load-bearing at all times, rather than only at completion?
status: Thousand-robot programmable self-assembly demonstrated large-scale planar shape formation (Rubenstein, Cornejo, and Nagpal (2014), *Programmable self-assembly in a thousand-robot swarm*, DOI:10.1126/science.1254295); load-bearing three-dimensional construction adds mechanical constraints that remain unaddressed.
solved_when: A multi-robot system demonstrates assembly and repair of three-dimensional structures with mechanical stability guaranteed throughout all intermediate configurations.
why: It enables adaptable structures and deployable infrastructure that can be built and maintained in place by robot swarms.
key_works: Rubenstein, Cornejo, and Nagpal (2014), *Programmable self-assembly in a thousand-robot swarm*, DOI:10.1126/science.1254295.

title: Reproducible swarm scaling in real environments
open: How do reliability, maintenance labor, communication, and useful throughput actually scale as physical robot swarms grow from tens to thousands of robots operating outside controlled arenas? A rigorous answer requires reproducible measurements of these quantities across that full size range in real environments, rather than in laboratory settings.
status: Large laboratory swarms, notably Rubenstein et al. (2014), *Programmable self-assembly in a thousand-robot swarm*, DOI:10.1126/science.1254295, establish feasibility at scale in controlled settings; however, field reliability and total support cost remain unmeasured and require separate longitudinal evidence.
solved_when: Reproducible empirical data exist covering swarms from tens to thousands of physical robots in real (non-arena) environments, quantifying how reliability, maintenance labor, communication, and useful throughput each scale with swarm size.
why: It tests whether the claimed advantages of swarm systems survive contact with operational overhead — if maintenance labor or failures grow too fast with fleet size, swarm benefits disappear in practice.
key_works: Rubenstein et al. (2014), *Programmable self-assembly in a thousand-robot swarm*, DOI:10.1126/science.1254295.

title: Tolerance-robust overconstrained mechanisms
open: Can we design useful overconstrained linkages whose mobility and load capacity survive realistic manufacturing errors, wear, and thermal distortion?
status: Exact algebraic mobility can depend on special geometric relations; robust realizability is a different question from ideal kinematic existence. Key work: Schicho (2022), *And Yet It Moves*, arXiv:2004.12635.
solved_when: A design methodology exists that yields overconstrained linkages retaining mobility and load capacity under realistic manufacturing tolerances, wear, and thermal distortion.
why: It converts elegant mechanism families into manufacturable robots.
key_works: Schicho (2022), *And Yet It Moves*, arXiv:2004.12635.

title: High-torque actuators with sustained thermal performance
open: Can an actuator be designed that delivers higher continuous torque density while still satisfying the full set of practical demands — efficiency, backdrivability, impact tolerance, and acceptable temperature — over realistic duty cycles?
status: Actuator architectures offer competing advantages; peak specifications do not settle sustained multi-objective performance. Key works: Vanderborght et al. (2013), *Variable impedance actuators: A review*, DOI:10.1016/j.robot.2013.06.009.
solved_when: An actuator design demonstrates improved continuous torque density while preserving efficiency, backdrivability, impact tolerance, and acceptable temperature over realistic duty cycles.
why: It determines the practical payload and endurance a robot can sustain, not just what its peak specifications promise.
key_works: Vanderborght et al. (2013), *Variable impedance actuators: A review*, DOI:10.1016/j.robot.2013.06.009.

title: Wide-band variable impedance with guaranteed passivity
open: Can a robot's actuation be made to vary its stiffness and damping rapidly and accurately over a wide range of operation, while provably dissipating rather than injecting energy at every impedance setting?
status: Variable-impedance and elastic actuation are established; bandwidth, range, efficiency, and stability remain coupled tradeoffs. The main reference point is Vanderborght et al. (2013), *Variable impedance actuators: A review*, DOI:10.1016/j.robot.2013.06.009.
solved_when: A design or control scheme is given that achieves wide-band, accurate stiffness and damping modulation across a broad operating range with a passivity guarantee — i.e., no contact destabilization and no uncontrolled energy injection at any point of the operating envelope.
why: It would allow robots to interact safely and compliantly with people and environments without paying for safety with slowness or weakness, which is the core coupling blocking capable physical interaction today.
key_works: Vanderborght et al. (2013), *Variable impedance actuators: A review*, DOI:10.1016/j.robot.2013.06.009.

title: Useful onboard power for small untethered robots
open: Can a small untethered robot carry enough onboard power to be genuinely useful, with energy storage, conversion, cooling, and distribution integrated without consuming the mass and volume needed for sensing and actuation?
status: Power remains one of the broad robotics challenges identified by Yang et al. (2018), *The grand challenges of Science Robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aar7650; component energy density alone does not determine usable system endurance. Related directions include structural batteries and microscale energy conversion.
solved_when: A small robot platform demonstrates integrated energy storage, conversion, cooling, and distribution whose combined mass and volume leave sufficient budget for sensing and actuation, yielding usable system endurance rather than merely high component energy density.
why: Solving this is what turns tethered demonstrations into robots that operate autonomously in the world.
key_works: Yang et al. (2018), *The grand challenges of Science Robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aar7650.

title: Co-design that optimizes lifetime usefulness
open: Can robot bodies, actuators, controllers, sensors, and manufacturing and repair considerations be optimized jointly for usefulness over a machine's entire lifetime, rather than for a score on a narrow simulated task?
status: Recent holistic co-design work explicitly identifies narrow objectives and simulation–reality gaps as limitations; see Stölzle et al. (2025/2026), *Soft yet Effective Robots via Holistic Co-Design*, arXiv:2505.03761.
solved_when: A co-design formulation and method exist that jointly optimize body, actuator, controller, sensing, manufacturability, repairability, and lifetime performance, and demonstrably avoid designs that excel in optimization but fail as usable machines.
why: It prevents designs that are optimal in simulation but fail as usable machines in the real world.
key_works: Stölzle et al. (2025/2026), *Soft yet Effective Robots via Holistic Co-Design*, arXiv:2505.03761.

title: Mechanically and semantically interchangeable robot modules
open: Can robot modules — actuators and sensors — be made interchangeable in a way that goes beyond matching electrical connectors, so that a swapped-in module automatically communicates its calibration, limits, failure modes, and control semantics? In other words, can physical replaceability be extended into automatic semantic compatibility?
status: Modularity already simplifies robot construction, but physical interchangeability of modules does not by itself preserve control behavior. Relevant background includes Vanderborght et al. (2013), *Variable impedance actuators: A review*, DOI:10.1016/j.robot.2013.06.009, and Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2*, arXiv:2211.07752.
solved_when: A replaceable actuator or sensor module can be physically swapped into a platform and automatically convey its calibration data, operational limits, failure modes, and control semantics without manual per-platform integration, preserving control behavior across the exchange.
why: It would cut repair labor and eliminate platform-specific integration work, making modular robot fleets genuinely maintainable rather than merely easy to assemble.
key_works: Vanderborght et al. (2013), *Variable impedance actuators: A review*, DOI:10.1016/j.robot.2013.06.009; Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2*, arXiv:2211.07752.

title: Observable state representations for continuum bodies
open: Can a soft, continuum robot's distributed shape, strain, and internal pressure be recovered from a practical number of sensor measurements, enough to support reliable feedback control?
status: Soft robots challenge finite-dimensional modeling; task-dependent reduced representations are useful but not universally sufficient. Background is given by Rus and Tolley (2015), *Design, fabrication and control of soft robots*, DOI:10.1038/nature14543; related topics include observability of distributed-parameter systems and reduced-order modeling.
solved_when: A method exists that reconstructs a sufficient state representation (shape, strain, and internal pressure) for control from a number of sensors that is practical rather than body-wide instrumentation, and this sufficiency is demonstrated for reliable feedback control.
why: It would enable feedback control of continuum bodies without instrumenting every part of the body.
key_works: Rus and Tolley (2015), *Design, fabrication and control of soft robots*, DOI:10.1038/nature14543.

title: Control through hysteresis and material aging
open: How can a soft robot be kept behaving accurately when its material response shifts with loading history, temperature, and age? Formally: find a control (or online adaptation) scheme that compensates for evolving, history- and age-dependent material dynamics without requiring frequent full retraining of the robot's model.
status: Soft-robot design and control already accommodate nonlinear materials, as surveyed in Rus and Tolley (2015), *Design, fabrication and control of soft robots*, DOI:10.1038/nature14543, but long-term history-dependent material changes remain a separate, unsolved challenge.
solved_when: A control strategy is demonstrated that maintains behaviorally accurate soft-robot performance under changes in loading history, temperature, and material age, without frequent full retraining.
why: It preserves repeatability and reliability of soft robots in practical, long-term use, where material properties drift over time.
key_works: Rus and Tolley (2015), *Design, fabrication and control of soft robots*, DOI:10.1038/nature14543.

title: Fully soft closed-loop autonomy
open: Can an entirely soft, untethered robot close the loop on its own — sensing its environment, making nontrivial decisions, and adapting its behavior — without any rigid electronic control components?
status: The Octobot demonstrated integrated, entirely soft autonomous operation (Wehner et al. (2016), *An integrated design and fabrication strategy for entirely soft, autonomous robots*, DOI:10.1038/nature19100); richer environmental feedback and programmable decision-making remain stronger, unmet targets.
solved_when: A fully soft untethered robot is demonstrated that integrates environmental sensing, nontrivial decision-making, and adaptive behavior, all without rigid electronic control.
why: It would let robots exploit extreme deformation and confinement — squeezing through spaces unsafe or inaccessible to stiff-bodied machines — while remaining safe on contact.
key_works: Wehner et al. (2016), *An integrated design and fabrication strategy for entirely soft, autonomous robots*, DOI:10.1038/nature19100.

title: Retraction of growing robots without buckling or entanglement
open: Can a long, deployed growing robot be retracted back through the same tortuous passages it navigated, without buckling, entanglement, or loss of steering and payload integrity? Formally, the goal is a controlled retraction mechanism that respects environmental contact limits while inverting the deployment mechanics of an eversion-based robot.
status: Growth-based navigation has been demonstrated as a distinctive access mechanism in Hawkes et al. (2017), *A soft robot that navigates its environment through growth*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aan3028; however, controlled, reusable retraction remains unsolved and imposes mechanical constraints different from those of growth, related to the stability of slender structures and inverse deployment mechanics.
solved_when: A working retraction system is demonstrated that pulls a grown robot back through its full deployed path in confined, tortuous environments while preserving steering capability and payload integrity and staying within contact-force limits on the environment, making the robot reusable over repeated grow–retract cycles.
why: It converts growing robots from single-use access tools into retrievable, reusable systems, which is essential for practical deployment in search, inspection, and medical scenarios where the robot must be recovered after the task.
key_works: Hawkes et al. (2017), *A soft robot that navigates its environment through growth*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aan3028.

title: Autonomous branching and tool delivery by growing robots
open: Can a growing robot autonomously navigate a branching passage by choosing its own routes, and deliver and operate useful tools at the destination? Formally, this requires integrating tip-growth navigation with route selection and sustained tool operation while managing distributed friction, pressure, and material supply.
status: Tip-growth navigation is demonstrated, per Hawkes et al. (2017), *A soft robot that navigates its environment through growth*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aan3028; branching decisions and sustained tool operation remain open, requiring integrated planning and mechanics.
solved_when: A growing robot demonstrates passage of branching routes with autonomous route selection and sustained delivery and operation of a useful tool, under integrated management of distributed friction, pressure, and material supply.
why: It would enable practical pipe inspection, confined-space repair, and minimally invasive access to spaces no conventional robot can reach.
key_works: Hawkes et al. (2017), *A soft robot that navigates its environment through growth*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aan3028.

title: Reproducible multimaterial soft-robot fabrication
open: Can soft robots built from multiple materials be manufactured so that their geometry, bonding, actuation, and lifetime are predictable across fabrication batches and across different laboratories?
status: Integrated multimaterial hands demonstrate promising fabrication; controlling production variation remains necessary for reproducible performance. Key work: Alves et al. (2023), *Integrated Design Fabrication and Control of a Bioinspired Multimaterial Soft Robotic Hand*, DOI:10.34133/cbsystems.0051.
solved_when: A fabrication process exists whose produced soft robots exhibit consistent geometry, bonding, actuation performance, and lifetime across batches and laboratories.
why: It moves soft robots from artisanal prototypes toward reliable products.
key_works: Alves et al. (2023), *Integrated Design Fabrication and Control of a Bioinspired Multimaterial Soft Robotic Hand*, DOI:10.34133/cbsystems.0051.

title: Soft-robot design with validated safety–performance tradeoffs
open: How do compliance, speed, payload, and contact geometry jointly determine both injury risk and task performance in soft robots, and how can these measured relationships be built directly into design optimization?
status: Holistic co-design work identifies safety and broader design values as unresolved integration issues; no validated quantification of these joint effects is yet incorporated into design optimization. Key work: Stölzle et al. (2025/2026), *Soft yet Effective Robots via Holistic Co-Design*, arXiv:2505.03761.
solved_when: A quantitative characterization of the joint effect of compliance, speed, payload, and contact geometry on injury and task performance exists, and those measurements are incorporated into a design-optimization procedure with validated safety–performance tradeoffs.
why: It prevents "soft" from being treated as a sufficient safety argument, replacing intuition with measurable safety–performance tradeoffs in the design loop.
key_works: Stölzle et al. (2025/2026), *Soft yet Effective Robots via Holistic Co-Design*, arXiv:2505.03761.

title: Load-bearing self-healing after mechanical damage
open: Can a load-bearing soft robot recover its ability to generate force, seal itself, and sense after being punctured or torn — and do so repeatably across multiple damage cycles while staying operational, rather than being repaired by hand between uses? Formally, the goal is an integrated self-healing mechanism that restores structural integrity and actuation/sensing function under mechanical damage without halting the robot.
status: The current state of the art is electrical self-healing in HASEL actuators (Acome et al. (2018), *Hydraulically amplified self-healing electrostatic actuators with muscle-like performance*, DOI:10.1126/science.aao6139), which addresses dielectric breakdown but is not equivalent to repairing arbitrary mechanical tears.
solved_when: A robot that remains operational after puncture or tearing demonstrates restored useful force, sealing, and sensing, with the healing repeatable over multiple damage cycles.
why: It would make soft robots viable in abrasive and hazardous environments where mechanical damage is routine and manual repair is impractical.
key_works: Acome et al. (2018), *Hydraulically amplified self-healing electrostatic actuators with muscle-like performance*, DOI:10.1126/science.aao6139.

title: Integrated microscale sensing, computation, and motion
open: Can we build microscopic robots that carry their own sensing, state estimation, decision-making, and actuation, so they operate without any external system tracking their state? Concretely, the goal is a mass-manufacturable microscopic robot integrating all of these functions on board.
status: Electronically integrated microscopic robots have been demonstrated with semiconductor-compatible fabrication (Miskin et al. (2020), *Electronically integrated, mass-manufactured, microscopic robots*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2626-9); complete useful autonomy, however, still requires additional integration.
solved_when: A mass-manufacturable microscopic robot demonstrates integrated on-board sensing, state estimation, decision-making, and actuation while operating without external state tracking.
why: It would unlock microscopic systems that do more than passively follow externally imposed fields, moving from field-driven motion toward genuine autonomy.
key_works: Miskin et al. (2020), *Electronically integrated, mass-manufactured, microscopic robots*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2626-9.

title: Power budgets for autonomous microscopic robots
open: What can an autonomous microscopic robot actually do when its energy supply and heat-dissipation budget are constrained by physics at that scale? More precisely, determine the sensing, computation, communication, and locomotion capabilities achievable under realistic microscopic energy and thermal limits.
status: Fabricated microscopic robots have established component feasibility, most notably in Miskin et al. (2020), *Electronically integrated, mass-manufactured, microscopic robots*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2626-9; however, end-to-end energy allocation remains a fundamental constraint.
solved_when: A characterization exists of which combinations of sensing, computation, communication, and locomotion capabilities are achievable within realistic microscopic energy-supply and heat-dissipation limits, distinguishing physically plausible architectures from impossible specifications.
why: It separates physically plausible microrobot architectures from impossible specifications, giving designers a principled basis for what to build.
key_works: Miskin et al. (2020), *Electronically integrated, mass-manufactured, microscopic robots*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2626-9.

title: Closed-loop navigation in moving biological fluids
open: How can a microrobot be navigated autonomously through flowing biological fluids past complex anatomical boundaries, using only clinically compatible sensing and actuation, while maintaining a quantified bound on localization error?
status: Biomedical microrobotics demonstrates many propulsion and guidance approaches, but closed-loop operation in realistic anatomy remains demanding. Key reference: Nelson, Kaliakatsos, and Abbott (2010), *Microrobots for Minimally Invasive Medicine*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-bioeng-010510-103409.
solved_when: A closed-loop navigation scheme is demonstrated that operates in realistic variable-flow anatomy with clinically compatible sensing and actuation and achieves a quantified localization error bound.
why: It would enable targeted interventions with less invasive access, moving microrobotics from laboratory propulsion demonstrations toward usable clinical procedures.
key_works: Nelson, Kaliakatsos, and Abbott (2010), *Microrobots for Minimally Invasive Medicine*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-bioeng-010510-103409.

title: Tracking microrobot swarms inside opaque tissue
open: How can individual or task-relevant collective states of microrobot swarms be resolved inside opaque tissue at adequate spatial and temporal resolution? Any answer must do so without imposing excessive imaging exposure or requiring instrumentation incompatible with in-vivo operation.
status: Biomedical microrobot reviews, notably Sitti et al.
