(2015), *Biomedical Applications of Untethered Mobile Milli/Microrobots*, DOI:10.1109/JPROC.2014.2385105, identify localization and imaging as essential enabling capabilities for the field. Related mathematical threads include super-resolution inverse problems and sparse tracking under limited observations.
solved_when: A method exists that resolves individual or task-relevant collective states within opaque tissue at spatial and temporal resolution adequate for the intended task, while keeping imaging exposure within acceptable limits and using instrumentation compatible with in-vivo biomedical use.
why: It makes closed-loop therapy and recovery verifiable: without adequate tracking, microrobot interventions inside the body cannot be monitored, controlled, or confirmed in real time.
key_works: Sitti et al. (2015), *Biomedical Applications of Untethered Mobile Milli/Microrobots*, DOI:10.1109/JPROC.2014.2385105.

title: Reliable clearance or retrieval after microrobot deployment
open: Can deployed microrobots be reliably cleared from the body after completing their task — retrieved intact, safely degraded, or otherwise eliminated — even in the worst case, without harmful residual material or byproducts?
status: Minimally invasive microrobotics establishes possible interventions, as surveyed in Nelson et al. (2010), *Microrobots for Minimally Invasive Medicine*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-bioeng-010510-103409, but the post-task fate of deployed devices remains a separate, unaddressed translational requirement.
solved_when: A demonstrated protocol shows that deployed devices are retrieved, degraded, or cleared, with quantified worst-case retention levels and accounting for material byproducts produced by degradation.
why: Without verified clearance, even a successfully executed medical task leaves unacceptable residual risk, blocking translation of microrobot interventions into clinical use.
key_works: Nelson et al. (2010), *Microrobots for Minimally Invasive Medicine*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-bioeng-010510-103409.

title: Reproducible biohybrid robot construction
open: Can biohybrid robots be built so that their morphology and behavior are reproducible from batch to batch, despite the inherent variability of their biological components? Formally, this asks for construction methods yielding consistent phenotypic and behavioral outcomes across independent production runs.
status: Reconfigurable-organism work demonstrates a design-to-realization pipeline; reliable manufacturing tolerances remain a broader target. Key work: Kriegman et al. (2020), *A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms*, DOI:10.1073/pnas.1910837117.
solved_when: A construction pipeline exists that produces biohybrid robots with reproducible morphology and behavior across batches, with quantified manufacturing tolerances stated for both.
why: Reproducibility would enable meaningful comparison between designs, dependable behavior in use, and controlled deployment of biohybrid systems.
key_works: Kriegman et al. (2020), *A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms*, DOI:10.1073/pnas.1910837117.

title: Long-term control of living robotic components
open: How can engineered systems maintain predictable function when their actuators are living organisms that grow, remodel, fatigue, and respond to their environment?
status: Biohybrid and living constructions demonstrate useful behavior, but stable long-duration input–output relationships are not automatic; no such framework is established. Key work: Kriegman et al. (2020), *A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms*, DOI:10.1073/pnas.1910837117.
solved_when: A control framework exists that preserves a stable, predictable input–output relationship in a biohybrid system over long durations despite growth, remodeling, fatigue, and environmental response of its living components.
why: It would make living components reliably usable in engineered systems rather than only in short-lived demonstrations.
key_works: Kriegman et al. (2020), *A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms*, DOI:10.1073/pnas.1910837117.

title: Year-scale useful underwater autonomy
open: Can an underwater robot sustain a defined scientific or inspection mission for a full year using only the replenishment infrastructure available at its operating site, with every intervention and maintenance event fully accounted for?
status: Long-duration marine platforms exist, but combining persistent sensing, manipulation, fouling management, and autonomous servicing remains a stronger integrated target than anything demonstrated. Key work: Yoerger et al. (2021), *A hybrid underwater robot for multidisciplinary investigation of the ocean twilight zone*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abe1901.
solved_when: A single integrated platform demonstrates a year-long mission with bounded human intervention, complete maintenance accounting, persistent sensing, manipulation, fouling management, and autonomous servicing.
why: It would enable continuous ocean observation without frequent ship support, replacing costly ship-dependent campaigns with persistent autonomous presence.
key_works: Yoerger et al. (2021), *A hybrid underwater robot for multidisciplinary investigation of the ocean twilight zone*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abe1901.

title: Underwater localization across changing acoustic conditions
open: How can an underwater robot keep track of where it is when turbid water blocks vision, acoustic propagation conditions shift over time, and the seafloor offers few stable landmarks? The goal is a localization method that stays accurate through these simultaneous sensing degradations.
status: Underwater robotic systems combine specialized sensing and navigation, but robust operation across simultaneous sensing degradations remains challenging. A representative capability milestone is Khatib et al. (2016), *Ocean One: A Robotic Avatar for Oceanic Discovery*, DOI:10.1109/MRA.2016.2613281. Related threads include acoustic inverse problems and navigation without global positioning.
solved_when: A localization system demonstrably maintains accurate position estimates under poor visibility, changing acoustic propagation, and sparse or mobile seafloor features — the combined condition, not each degradation in isolation.
why: Reliable localization under degraded sensing is what enables precise inspection, sampling, and manipulation in the ocean, where GPS is unavailable and conditions change constantly.
key_works: Khatib et al. (2016), *Ocean One: A Robotic Avatar for Oceanic Discovery*, DOI:10.1109/MRA.2016.2613281.

title: Under-ice exploration with guaranteed return opportunities
open: Explore beneath moving or irregular ice while preserving a defensible route to a recoverable exit despite limited communication and uncertain currents.
status: Ice-world robotic exploration motivates autonomous navigation in confined, hazardous environments, and practical return guarantees require explicit environmental assumptions.
solved_when: A planning framework is given that navigates under such ice while maintaining, at every step, a guaranteed return path to an exit point, under explicitly stated environmental assumptions.
why: It makes otherwise inaccessible scientific missions under ice far less likely to lose the vehicle.
key_works: Vaquero et al. (2024), *EELS: Autonomous snake-like robot with task and motion planning capabilities for ice world exploration*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adh8332.

title: Dexterous manipulation at extreme ocean pressure
open: Can a robot perform precise, force-sensitive manipulation at the extreme pressures of the hadal zone? The goal is a dexterous manipulation system combining durable sensing, actuation, sealing, and pressure-compatible materials that operates at such depths.
status: A self-powered soft robot has operated in the Mariana Trench (Li et al. (2021), *Self-powered soft robot in the Mariana Trench*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-03153-z), but dexterous manipulation at comparable pressure remains a substantially richer target.
solved_when: A demonstrated system performs precise, force-sensitive manipulation at hadal pressures with durable sensing, actuation, sealing, and pressure-compatible materials.
why: It unlocks deep-ocean sampling and intervention on deep-sea infrastructure, tasks currently beyond existing deep-sea platforms.
key_works: Li et al. (2021), *Self-powered soft robot in the Mariana Trench*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-03153-z.

title: Non-disruptive tracking of fragile marine organisms
open: Can an underwater robot track and observe fragile marine organisms over time without altering the very behavior it is meant to study — that is, with disturbance from its illumination, sound, flow, heat, and physical proximity all kept below quantified thresholds?
status: Mesobot was designed for twilight-zone biological investigation; quantitatively proving minimal disturbance across species remains a further experimental target. Key work: Yoerger et al. (2021), *A hybrid underwater robot for multidisciplinary investigation of the ocean twilight zone*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abe1901.
solved_when: A robot demonstrably follows and observes target organisms while bounding each disturbance source — illumination, sound, flow, heat, and physical proximity — at experimentally validated, quantitatively minimal levels across species.
why: Without such bounds, robotic observation changes the behavior being studied, so the resulting ecological measurements are biased by the observer itself.
key_works: Yoerger et al. (2021), *A hybrid underwater robot for multidisciplinary investigation of the ocean twilight zone*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abe1901.

title: Coordinated sampling of evolving water parcels
open: How can a fleet of autonomous underwater robots stay aligned with a single evolving water parcel over time, so that measured changes in its biology can be attributed to actual biological processes rather than to transport or sampling bias?
status: Coordinated autonomous Lagrangian microbial studies have been demonstrated in Zhang et al. (2021), *A system of coordinated autonomous robots for Lagrangian studies of microbes in the oceanic deep chlorophyll maximum*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abb9138; broader spatiotemporal coverage and uncertainty accounting remain open.
solved_when: A multi-robot system demonstrably tracks a changing water mass with coordinated sampling, and provides spatiotemporal coverage and uncertainty accounting sufficient to separate biological evolution from transport effects and sampling bias.
why: Without such separation, ocean biological measurements cannot be causally interpreted — apparent changes could be artifacts of advection or uneven sampling rather than real microbial dynamics.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2021), *A system of coordinated autonomous robots for Lagrangian studies of microbes in the oceanic deep chlorophyll maximum*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abb9138.

title: Deep-sea soft robots with long-lived useful payloads
open: Can a deep-sea soft robot carry useful payloads — sensors, communication systems, and task equipment — while keeping pressure-tolerant locomotion reliable across repeated dives?
status: Pressure-tolerant soft locomotion has been demonstrated by operation in the Mariana Trench (Li et al. (2021), *Self-powered soft robot in the Mariana Trench*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-03153-z), but payload integration and service life remain separate, unmet requirements.
solved_when: A soft robot demonstrates pressure-tolerant locomotion integrated with sustained sensing, communication, and task payloads, maintaining reliable operation over repeated dives.
why: It would turn an extreme-environment demonstration into a practical scientific platform for deep-ocean work.
key_works: Li et al. (2021), *Self-powered soft robot in the Mariana Trench*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-03153-z.

title: Autonomous underwater repair and connector mating
open: Can an autonomous underwater robot carry out a full repair intervention — inspecting, cleaning, aligning, mating, and verifying a wet connector or repair interface — on its own despite currents, biofouling, low visibility, and uncertain contact forces?
status: Ocean One (Khatib et al. (2016), *Ocean One*, DOI:10.1109/MRA.2016.2613281) demonstrates underwater dexterous interaction, but complete autonomous servicing remains open because it additionally requires diagnosis and verification.
solved_when: A robotic system autonomously completes the entire servicing sequence of inspection, cleaning, alignment, mating, and verification on underwater connectors or repair interfaces, with diagnosis and verification included, under realistic environmental disturbances.
why: It removes the need for human divers and costly dedicated intervention vessels, making routine subsea maintenance practical.
key_works: Khatib et al. (2016), *Ocean One*, DOI:10.1109/MRA.2016.2613281.

title: Reliable anchoring and mobility in microgravity
open: How can a robot move across and manipulate the surface of a small solar-system body whose cohesion and gravity are poorly known, without escaping, overturning, or destabilizing the surface it is working on? Formally, this asks for anchoring and mobility strategies whose failure modes (escape trajectories, tip-over, surface disruption) are bounded under uncertainty in the granular contact mechanics of weak-gravity environments.
status: Small-body exploration currently faces poorly constrained surface mechanics, since terrestrial contact assumptions do not transfer directly to microgravity environments. Key work: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.
solved_when: A demonstrated method — validated experimentally, given the problem's experimental type — for locomotion, anchoring, and manipulation on small-body surfaces that reliably avoids escape, overturning, and surface destabilization under uncertain cohesion and gravity conditions.
why: It enables repeated sampling and instrument placement on small bodies, the core operations of scientific exploration missions.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.

title: Predictive regolith interaction models
open: Can a robot predict how unfamiliar regolith will respond — sinkage, traction, excavation forces, and ejecta — from only sparse measurements, with quantified uncertainty on those predictions? A transferable predictive model of granular–vehicle interaction that generalizes across regolith environments remains the target.
status: Unexpected surface interactions encountered in planetary exploration motivate both autonomy and improved physical characterization of regolith; a transferable predictive model remains a key target, per Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.
solved_when: A predictive model quantifies sinkage, traction, excavation forces, and ejecta on unfamiliar regolith, with calibrated uncertainty derived from sparse in-situ measurements and demonstrated transfer across environments.
why: Such a model prevents vehicle immobilization on poorly characterized terrain and enables reliable resource extraction.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.

title: Autonomous exploration of planetary crevasses and caves
open: Can a robotic system autonomously enter, map, and sample an unknown confined planetary terrain — a crevasse or cave — and reliably return, despite contact-rich locomotion, intermittent communications, finite energy, and failure states it cannot reach to fix? Formally, this asks for integrated autonomy across entry, mapping, sampling, and recovery under uncertainty in terrain whose topology is unknown a priori.
status: EELS demonstrates integrated autonomy for ice-world exploration scenarios, as reported in Vaquero et al. (2024), *EELS*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adh8332; complete extraterrestrial mission qualification remains a broader target.
solved_when: A system demonstrates entry, mapping, sampling, and recovery from unknown confined terrain while managing contact, communications, energy, and inaccessible failure states — up to the standard of complete extraterrestrial mission qualification.
why: It opens access to protected geology and potentially habitable environments that no current asset can reach.
key_works: Vaquero et al. (2024), *EELS*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adh8332.

title: Onboard scientific novelty assessment
open: Can a spacecraft's onboard systems reliably judge which observations and samples are scientifically valuable, telling genuine novelty apart from sensor artifacts or model failures?
status: Space autonomy research covers planning and scientific operations, but robust autonomous scientific judgment remains more demanding than navigation. Nesnas, Fesq, and Volpe (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.
solved_when: An autonomous system demonstrates selection of scientifically valuable observations and samples while reliably distinguishing genuine novelty from sensor artifacts and model failure.
why: It increases scientific return when bandwidth constraints and communication delays limit human oversight during missions.
key_works: Nesnas, Fesq, and Volpe (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.

title: Autonomous spacecraft inspection and repair
open: Can a robotic spacecraft autonomously handle an unfamiliar external fault end to end — diagnosing it, planning physical access, performing a bounded repair, and verifying success — while contending with orbital dynamics and delayed human supervision?
status: Space robotics currently supports inspection and servicing concepts, but integrated diagnosis-to-repair autonomy remains a larger capability. Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.
solved_when: A demonstrated system diagnoses an unfamiliar external fault, plans physical access, performs a bounded repair, and verifies success, all under orbital dynamics and delayed human supervision.
why: It extends spacecraft life and reduces the need for replacement missions.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.

title: Capture of uncooperative objects with unknown inertia
open: How can a robotic spacecraft safely grasp a tumbling, uncooperative object whose inertia properties, flexible appendages, contact mechanics, and residual motion are all unknown? Formally, this asks for a principled solution to the coupled estimation–control problem in which the target's dynamics must be identified online while contact is established, without endangering either vehicle.
status: Space manipulation research addresses rendezvous and contact, but unknown target dynamics make safe capture a coupled estimation–control problem that remains unresolved. Related work includes adaptive capture dynamics and momentum management; see Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.
solved_when: A provably safe capture strategy exists for targets with unknown inertia and uncertain contact and flexibility properties, accounting for residual tumbling motion; success is measured by safe, stable capture under the stated uncertainties.
why: It directly enables debris removal and on-orbit servicing of failed spacecraft, where the target cannot be instrumented or cooperative.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.

title: Shared qualification pathways for high-risk space autonomy
open: Can the space robotics community build shared qualification pathways — reusable physical tests, datasets, and flight opportunities — through which new autonomy methods accumulate credible evidence without each project financing a complete mission?
status: EELS illustrates the scale of integrated field validation; the proposed gap is reusable qualification infrastructure, not a claim that existing programs are absent (Vaquero et al. (2024), *EELS*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adh8332).
solved_when: Standing infrastructure exists for reusable physical tests, datasets, and flight opportunities that new autonomy projects can use to accumulate credible evidence toward mission eligibility, without individually funding full missions.
why: It lowers the barrier between laboratory autonomy and mission eligibility, so promising methods can be qualified rather than stalled for lack of mission-scale funding.
key_works: Vaquero et al. (2024), *EELS*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adh8332.

title: Navigation through simultaneous dust, smoke, and darkness
open: Can a robot keep localized and aware of obstacles when dust, smoke, and darkness degrade all of its sensing modalities at once — including the dust clouds the robot itself kicks up while moving? More formally, how do we preserve navigation performance under correlated, common-cause degradation of vision, lidar, and related sensors rather than the failure of any single modality?
status: Systems such as NeBula (Agha et al. (2021), *NeBula: Quest for Robotic Autonomy in Challenging Environments*, arXiv:2103.11470) and CERBERUS (Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067) demonstrate difficult subterranean autonomy, but correlated sensing failures — multiple modalities degrading together — remain a harder operational regime that current systems do not fully address.
solved_when: A navigation system demonstrates sustained localization and obstacle detection through simultaneous dust, smoke, and darkness — including robot-induced dust clouds — at a level comparable to normal sensing conditions, evaluated in realistic subterranean or disaster-response environments.
why: It enables emergency responders to send robots where ordinary visual navigation fails entirely, providing access and situational awareness in environments too dangerous or degraded for humans.
key_works: Agha et al. (2021), *NeBula: Quest for Robotic Autonomy in Challenging Environments*, arXiv:2103.11470; Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067.

title: Communication infrastructure that deploys itself
open: When can a team of robots, exploring an unknown subterranean or disaster environment, decide on its own where to place communication relays so that connectivity is preserved without giving up too much exploration ability and without relying on a known radio map? Formally, characterize joint exploration–relay-deployment policies that maintain useful communication under uncertain propagation and changing network topology.
status: Subterranean systems, such as NeBila (Agha et al., 2021, arXiv:2103.11470), explicitly manage communications, but optimal deployment under uncertain propagation and changing topology remains difficult.
solved_when: A policy exists (with guarantees) that jointly explores and places relays while preserving useful communication and without assuming a known radio map or sacrificing too much exploration capacity.
why: It extends autonomy into tunnels and collapsed structures, where human infrastructure and operators cannot go.
key_works: Agha et al. (2021), *NeBula*, arXiv:2103.11470.

title: Traversability assessment for collapse-prone terrain
open: Can a robot determine whether rubble, a floor, a ladder, or a covering will support it — without performing an unsafe full-load test? Formally, the goal is active, nondestructive inference of load-bearing capacity of terrain and structures ahead of contact, using onboard sensing and controlled mechanical interaction.
status: Legged subterranean exploration, as in Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067, demonstrates mobility through difficult terrain, but hidden structural integrity remains unaddressed and requires additional sensing and mechanics.
solved_when: A method exists that reliably predicts whether a candidate surface can bear the robot's weight before the robot commits its full load, avoiding both robot loss and secondary collapse, and validated experimentally on collapse-prone terrain.
why: It prevents the loss of robots and secondary collapse of structures, which is critical when the robot itself is the rescue or reconnaissance asset.
key_works: Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067.

title: Victim search with calibrated missed-detection risk
open: How should a robot plan search coverage when its ability to detect a human victim varies realistically — through occlusion, competing heat sources, sound interference, and degrading sensor performance? Formally, the goal is a search planner that reasons over a calibrated probability of missed detection rather than treating coverage of the map as a proxy for finding people.
status: Subterranean exploration and object search provide relevant foundations — e.g., Agha et al. (2021), *NeBula*, arXiv:2103.11470 — but human rescue needs calibrated false-negative risk rather than map coverage alone; related work exists in search theory and detection probability under censored observations.
solved_when: A search planner demonstrably produces coverage plans whose claimed missed-detection risk is calibrated against actual detection outcomes under occlusion, heat-source clutter, sound interference, and changing sensor performance.
why: It makes "searched" a defensible operational claim, so responders can trust that a robot-cleared area genuinely carries quantified residual risk rather than mere map coverage.
key_works: Agha et al. (2021), *NeBula*, arXiv:2103.11470.

title: Manipulating rubble without destabilizing the scene
open: Can a robot autonomously remove or reposition rubble in a collapsed structure while predicting how the support configuration of the scene will change, so that its actions never trigger a secondary collapse, injure a trapped person, or block an escape route?
status: Field mobility is more mature than autonomous structural intervention; contact-rich scene modification adds consequential hidden mechanics. Key works: Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067; Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*, arXiv:2010.01083.
solved_when: A robot system can execute debris manipulation with an explicit prediction of resulting support changes and a verified guarantee of avoiding secondary collapse, harm to trapped persons, and blocked escape routes.
why: It moves disaster-response robots from passive reconnaissance toward physically assisting victims, which is the step that makes them useful on scene rather than merely observational.
key_works: Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067; Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*, arXiv:2010.01083.

title: Tether and cable management in unknown spaces
open: How can a tethered robot navigate an unknown, cluttered space while actively managing its cable — avoiding snagging, excessive tension, abrasion, and topological entrapment — so that it can reliably retrace its path and recover? Formally, this asks for motion planning and control policies that treat the tether's evolving configuration as a controllable state rather than a passive constraint.
status: Work on confined-space robotic access has demonstrated the value of specialized robot bodies for such environments; however, the tether itself adds a deformable object whose state must be controlled continuously, and this remains unaddressed. A relevant reference point is Hawkes et al. (2017), *A soft robot that navigates its environment through growth*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aan3028; related threads include cable topology and elastic-rod planning.
solved_when: A tethered robot demonstrates navigation in an unknown environment with no snagging, abrasion, or excess-tension events, plus reliable retracing and recovery of its path — with the tether state continuously controlled throughout.
why: It would make powered and communication-tethered robotic systems operationally reliable in confined and hazardous spaces, where a tangled or snapped tether currently ends the mission.
key_works: Hawkes et al. (2017), *A soft robot that navigates its environment through growth*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aan3028.

title: Hazard mapping without entering intolerable exposure
open: Can a robot map hazardous gas sources and concentration boundaries without ever entering regions of intolerable exposure, even when its own motion disturbs the plume and its sensors report delayed readings? Formally, this asks for exploration and localization strategies that remain within platform operating limits under sensor delay and robot-induced plume disturbance.
status: Mobile gas localization research has so far focused on source finding; adding simultaneous exposure-constrained exploration introduces a new safety requirement. Key work: Francis et al. (2022), *Gas source localization and mapping with mobile robots: A review*, DOI:10.1002/rob.22109.
solved_when: A mapping and source-localization method is demonstrated that accounts for sensor delay and robot-induced plume disturbance while provably keeping the platform within its operating limits throughout the mission.
why: It enables safer industrial and emergency reconnaissance by allowing hazards to be characterized without putting robots or operators at unacceptable risk.
key_works: Francis et al. (2022), *Gas source localization and mapping with mobile robots: A review*, DOI:10.1002/rob.22109.

title: Rapid deployment by nonexpert response teams
open: Can responders who have never met the robot get it mission-ready — transport, initialize, supervise, and recover it — under incident time pressure, entirely without support from the research team that built it?
status: Challenging field systems, such as Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067, demonstrate integrated capability, but their deployment burden and operator dependence have not been validated and require separate acceptance testing.
solved_when: A field demonstration shows trained but unfamiliar operators completing the full deployment cycle (transport, initialization, supervision, recovery) within the required time budget, unassisted by developers.
why: This is what determines whether such robots are actually useful during real incidents rather than only in research demonstrations.
key_works: Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067.

title: Hidden-peduncle localization and cutting
open: Can a robot reliably find and cut the correct fruit attachment point when it is hidden by leaves, the plant is moving, and neighboring stems look similar — without bruising or otherwise damaging the crop?
status: Harvesting robots demonstrate crop-specific success; system-level reviews continue to identify occlusion and perception-to-action errors as open failure modes, as surveyed in Bac et al. (2014), *Harvesting Robots for High-value Crops: State-of-the-art Review and Challenges Ahead*, DOI:10.1002/rob.21525.
solved_when: The robot localizes the hidden peduncle and completes the cut under occlusion, plant motion, and adjacent stems, with no crop damage.
why: It raises harvest completion rates and cuts down on crop damage, directly improving the viability of autonomous harvesting.
key_works: Bac et al. (2014), *Harvesting Robots for High-value Crops: State-of-the-art Review and Challenges Ahead*, DOI:10.1002/rob.21525.

title: Predicting delayed bruising from robotic handling
open: Can a robot's handling history — contact forces together with ripeness, temperature, and cultivar — be used to predict the bruising and quality loss that only appears days after harvest? In other words, can delayed damage be estimated as it happens, rather than assessed only through visible immediate damage?
status: A 2026 system-level harvesting review emphasizes quality and full-process evaluation, noting that delayed damage requires longitudinal measurement. Key work: Wang et al. (2026), *System-Level Smart Robotic Harvesting for High-Value Greenhouse Crops: A Review*, DOI:10.3390/agronomy16181795.
solved_when: A validated predictive model combines contact history, ripeness, temperature, and cultivar to estimate later quality loss, verified by longitudinal measurement of delayed damage rather than immediate visual inspection alone.
why: It prevents a harvest that looks successful from destroying saleable value: damage that surfaces after sale currently goes undetected at picking time.
key_works: Wang et al. (2026), *System-Level Smart Robotic Harvesting for High-Value Greenhouse Crops: A Review*, DOI:10.3390/agronomy16181795.

title: Ripeness estimation that transfers across cultivars
open: Can a robot estimate how ripe a crop is — and its internal quality — in a way that carries over across cultivars, seasons, lighting, and growing conditions? Formally, the goal is a transferable biological-state estimator with calibrated uncertainty over that full range of variation.
status: Agricultural robotics currently uses multiple sensing approaches, but transferable biological-state estimation remains more difficult than appearance classification. Key work: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics: The Future of Robotic Agriculture*, arXiv:1806.06762.
solved_when: Ripeness and internal-quality estimates remain accurate across cultivars, seasons, lighting, and growing conditions, with uncertainty that is calibrated under that distribution shift, demonstrated experimentally.
why: Reliable transfer enables selective harvesting at the right time, so robots pick each item when it is actually ready rather than when it merely looks ready.
key_works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics: The Future of Robotic Agriculture*, arXiv:1806.06762.

title: Selective weeding among touching or overlapping plants
open: Can a robot safely remove weeds in a field where weeds and crops physically touch or overlap, with unfamiliar plant shapes and imperfect localization? Formally, this asks for selective intervention that achieves weed removal while never causing irreversible damage to crop plants under these conditions.
status: Agricultural robots address weed control, but robust discrimination and precise intervention in dense mixed growth remain difficult; see Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762.
solved_when: A demonstrated system discriminates crops from weeds among touching or overlapping plants with unfamiliar morphology and removes the weeds while preserving the crops, tolerating localization errors without irreversible crop damage.
why: It would reduce herbicide use without sacrificing crop yield.
key_works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762.

title: Robotic pollination with measured ecological consequences
open: Can a robotic system pollinate crops effectively while simultaneously measuring the ecological consequences of its own intervention? In particular, can it quantify flower damage, plant reproductive outcomes, pathogen transfer, and effects on natural pollinators, rather than merely achieving successful contact with flowers?
status: Agricultural automation creates intervention opportunities, but successful contact with flowers is not sufficient evidence of agronomic or ecological benefit. Key works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762.
solved_when: A robotic pollination system demonstrates effective pollination in the field with measured outcomes for flower damage, reproductive success, pathogen transfer, and impacts on natural pollinators.
why: It separates a mechanical demonstration from a useful agricultural intervention: without these measurements, successful flower contact is not evidence of agronomic or ecological benefit.
key_works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762.

title: Robotic phenotyping without selection bias
open: Can a field robot estimate crop traits without systematically missing the plants that are occluded, damaged, unusually shaped, or hard for it to reach? In formal terms, can trait estimates be made statistically unbiased for the full plant population despite accessibility-dependent sampling?
status: Field robotics enables repeated measurement, but accessibility-dependent sampling can bias the inferred biological population. Related to missing-not-at-random inference and unbiased biological sampling; key work includes Bac et al. (2014), *Harvesting Robots for High-value Crops*, DOI:10.1002/rob.21525.
solved_when: A robotic phenotyping method is demonstrated to estimate crop traits over the full plant population without systematic bias from occlusion, damage, atypical morphology, or limited accessibility; no quantitative targets are specified in the record.
why: It makes robotic measurements trustworthy inputs for breeding and agronomic decisions; without correcting the bias, accessibility-dependent sampling distorts the inferred biological population.
key_works: Bac et al. (2014), *Harvesting Robots for High-value Crops*, DOI:10.1002/rob.21525.

title: Mobility that minimizes soil compaction
open: How should an agricultural robot plan its movement across a field when soil moisture, bearing strength, and crop-root sensitivity are uncertain, so that it still meets its work and energy requirements? Formally, the goal is a motion-planning construction that minimizes soil compaction under these uncertainties while satisfying stated work and energy constraints.
status: Agricultural robotics currently motivates lighter and more precise machinery, but measuring and optimizing cumulative soil effects remains a separate target (Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762).
solved_when: A planning method is produced that accounts for uncertain soil moisture, bearing strength, and crop-root sensitivity, minimizes cumulative soil compaction effects, and satisfies the work and energy requirements of the agricultural task.
why: It prevents the labor savings of agricultural automation from being paid for through long-term soil damage.
key_works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762.

title: Hygienic food manipulation with reliable recovery
open: Can a robotic system manipulate variable, delicate food items end-to-end while staying hygienic — and recover robustly when things go wrong? Formally, the goal is a food-handling system that maintains cleanability and contamination controls throughout operation and reliably recovers from dropped items, damaged packaging, and fouled grippers.
status: Harvesting and food manipulation currently show task-specific capability, but full-process quality, verification, and recovery remain system-level challenges. Wang et al. (2026), *System-Level Smart Robotic Harvesting for High-Value Greenhouse Crops: A Review*, DOI:10.3390/agronomy16181795.
solved_when: A demonstrated system handles variable food items across full-process operation while maintaining cleanability and contamination controls, including verified recovery from drops, damaged packaging, and fouled grippers.
why: It would turn today's isolated handling demonstrations into practical food automation, with system-level quality and verification rather than task-specific tricks.
key_works: Wang et al. (2026), *System-Level Smart Robotic Harvesting for High-Value Greenhouse Crops: A Review*, DOI:10.3390/agronomy16181795.

title: Assembly from unfamiliar parts and instructions
open: Can a robot assemble a product it has never seen before, given only the parts and instructions, without hand-written motion scripts or precisely staged starting conditions? In other words, achieve unrestricted new-product assembly transfer rather than performance on pre-specified tasks.
status: FurnitureBench provides reproducible long-horizon assembly tasks, but unrestricted new-product transfer remains a stronger, unmet target. Key work: Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench: Reproducible Real-World Benchmark for Long-Horizon Complex Manipulation*, arXiv:2305.12821.
solved_when: A robot system assembles a previously unseen product from its parts and instructions alone, with no manually authored motion scripts and no precisely staged initial conditions.
why: It would make high-mix, low-volume manufacturing economically viable, since robots could be retargeted to new products without per-product engineering.
key_works: Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench: Reproducible Real-World Benchmark for Long-Horizon Complex Manipulation*, arXiv:2305.12821.

title: Tight-tolerance insertion under uncertain geometry
open: Can a robot reliably complete tight-tolerance insertions when the parts, calibration, and friction are not exactly as modeled? That is, achieve robust insertion under part variation, imperfect calibration, compliance, and uncertain friction, without damaging the parts through repeated search motions.
status: Learned fine-grained manipulation demonstrates useful insertion-like skills, but robust tolerance handling requires explicit contact reasoning. Key work: Zhao et al. (2023), *Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware*, arXiv:2304.13705.
solved_when: A robotic system completes insertions with small clearances under part variation, imperfect calibration, compliance, and uncertain friction, while avoiding damaging search motions; no quantitative targets are stated, so success is a demonstrated reliable insertion across such uncertainties.
why: It would expand robotic assembly beyond settings that depend on precision fixtures, allowing assembly-grade manipulation with imperfect parts and setups.
key_works: Zhao et al. (2023), *Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware*, arXiv:2304.13705.

title: Complete wiring-harness installation
open: Can a robotic system autonomously complete a full wiring-harness installation — routing, fastening, connecting, inspecting, and correcting harnesses with flexible branches and visually similar connectors in confined assemblies?
status: Research has addressed individual deformable-object manipulation operations, as surveyed in Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767; complete installation remains open because it combines topology, force control, and electrical verification.
solved_when: A system performs the complete installation end-to-end: routing, fastening, connector mating, and inspection with correction of errors, on harnesses with flexible branches and visually similar connectors in confined assemblies.
why: Wiring-harness installation is a persistent labor-intensive manufacturing operation that resists automation, so a complete solution would remove a major manual bottleneck in production.
key_works: Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767.

title: Damage-aware disassembly for reuse
open: Can a robotic system disassemble an unfamiliar, previously used product when it cannot know the product's history — dealing with hidden fasteners, corrosion, adhesive bonds, and prior damage — while still preserving the valuable components for reuse?
status: Assembly benchmarks such as Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench*, arXiv:2305.12821, provide reusable manipulation foundations, but used-product disassembly adds the difficulties of uncertain history and destructive alternatives.
solved_when: A system demonstrates disassembly of unfamiliar used products under hidden fasteners, corrosion, adhesive bonds, and prior damage, preserving valuable components for reuse.
why: It enables remanufacturing and higher-value recycling, turning used products into recoverable assets rather than scrap.
key_works: Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench*, arXiv:2305.12821.

title: Closed-loop construction with variable local materials
open: Can a robotic construction system fabricate complete structures from materials whose properties drift during production, while continuously verifying geometry and structural performance as the build proceeds?
status: The Digital Construction Platform (Keating et al. (2017), *Toward site-specific and self-sufficient robotic fabrication on architectural scales*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aam8986) demonstrated architectural-scale on-site fabrication; adaptive structural qualification remains a broader target.
solved_when: A working system fabricates architectural-scale structures on site using variable local materials and demonstrates in-process verification of both geometry and structural performance as construction proceeds.
why: It would enable construction outside tightly controlled factories, where material consistency cannot be assumed.
key_works: Keating et al. (2017), *Toward site-specific and self-sufficient robotic fabrication on architectural scales*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aam8986.

title: Construction sequences that remain stable at every step
open: Can we plan a full construction sequence — the order of component placement together with the positioning of temporary supports — so that every intermediate structure is structurally stable under realistic disturbances such as placement error, wind, and uncertain material properties? Formally, the goal is a sequence of assembly actions whose every prefix yields a statically stable structure under a specified uncertainty model.
status: Termite-inspired construction, per Werfel, Petersen, and Nagpal (2014), *Designing Collective Behavior in a Termite-Inspired Robot Construction Team*, DOI:10.1126/science.1245842, demonstrates decentralized building; general structural stability throughout assembly is a stronger requirement that this work does not address.
solved_when: A method exists that, given a target structure and disturbance model (placement error, wind, uncertain material properties), outputs an assembly and temporary-support plan for which stability of every intermediate stage can be verified; short of a full method, a construction-sequence formulation with provable at-every-step stability under the stated disturbances counts as progress.
why: It prevents collapse during automated construction, which is the central safety barrier to deploying autonomous building systems outside controlled settings.
key_works: Werfel, Petersen, and Nagpal (2014), *Designing Collective Behavior in a Termite-Inspired Robot Construction Team*, DOI:10.1126/science.1245842.

title: Logistics fleets that recover from physical exceptions
open: Can an automated logistics fleet restore useful material flow after physical exceptions—shifted pallets, damaged packaging, fallen goods, blocked aisles, or failed docking—rather than merely replanning routes around a static obstacle?
status: Existing multi-agent pathfinding work addresses coordinated movement (Stern et al. (2019), *Multi-Agent Pathfinding*, arXiv:1906.08291), and integrated task and motion planning offers relevant machinery (Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*); however, operational exceptions typically require physical manipulation and workflow repair, which current approaches do not address.
solved_when: A system is demonstrated that detects such physical exceptions and recovers normal workflow through manipulation and workflow repair, not just coordinated replanning, thereby reducing the human exception-handling burden in automated facilities.
why: It directly cuts the human intervention load that currently bottlenecks fully automated warehouses and fulfillment operations.
key_works: Stern et al. (2019), *Multi-Agent Pathfinding*, arXiv:1906.08291; Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*.

title: Human–robot production that improves actual worker outcomes
open: Can human–robot production systems be optimized so that throughput improves together with, rather than at the expense of, worker fatigue, musculoskeletal load, workload variability, and worker control — measured over real shifts rather than brief laboratory trials?
status: A 2024 review (Haney and Liang (2024), *A literature review on safety perception and trust during human-robot interaction with autonomous mobile robots that apply to industrial environments*, DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537) found substantial gaps between laboratory HRI studies and industrial mobile-robot use.
solved_when: A system demonstrates joint optimization of throughput with fatigue, musculoskeletal load, workload variability, and worker control, with outcomes measured over real shifts rather than short laboratory trials.
why: It prevents efficiency gains from concealing ergonomic burdens displaced onto workers.
key_works: Haney and Liang (2024), *A literature review on safety perception and trust during human-robot interaction with autonomous mobile robots that apply to industrial environments*, DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537.

title: Tissue-damage-aware autonomous manipulation
open: Can an autonomous surgical robot regulate its interaction with soft tissue using patient-specific estimates of tearing, ischemia, crushing, and deformation limits, rather than relying on generic force thresholds? In other words, can safe tissue interaction be grounded in inferred, patient-specific material and anatomical models?
status: Surgical autonomy has been demonstrated on selected tasks, but safe tissue interaction remains an open challenge due to variation in anatomy and tissue material properties; current approaches do not yet replace generic force thresholds with patient-specific damage models. Key work: Attanasio et al. (2021), *Autonomy in Surgical Robotics*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-062420-090543.
solved_when: An autonomous manipulation system demonstrates control of tissue interaction governed by patient-specific estimates of tearing, ischemia, crushing, and deformation limits, replacing generic force thresholds as the safety-enforcing mechanism.
why: It would make surgical autonomy medically meaningful rather than merely geometrically accurate — safe in the sense of preventing tissue damage, not just precise in motion.
key_works: Attanasio et al. (2021), *Autonomy in Surgical Robotics*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-062420-090543.

title: Generalization across unfamiliar anatomy
open: Can an autonomous surgical robot execute a defined procedure reliably across clinically relevant anatomical variation, disease states, and visual conditions it was not selected for? A complete answer requires calibrated limits — the system should know when it is out of distribution — and a safe escalation path when those limits are reached.
status: SRT-H demonstrates long-horizon surgical steps and generalization in experimental settings (Kim et al. (2025), *SRT-H: A Hierarchical Framework for Autonomous Surgery via Language Conditioned Imitation Learning*, arXiv:2505.10251; DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adt5254); broad clinical coverage remains a stronger target than current systems achieve.
solved_when: The system executes the defined procedure across the full range of clinically relevant anatomical variation, disease states, and visual conditions specified, while correctly calibrating its competence limits and escalating (rather than proceeding) outside them.
why: Without generalization of this kind, autonomous surgical systems remain dependent on narrowly selected anatomical examples and cannot be trusted on the unselected variation real patients present.
key_works: Kim et al. (2025), *SRT-H: A Hierarchical Framework for Autonomous Surgery via Language Conditioned Imitation Learning*, arXiv:2505.10251; DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adt5254.

title: Autonomous verification of surgical completion
open: Can a surgical robot autonomously confirm that a step of an operation achieved its intended physiological result, rather than merely inferring success from how the instruments moved? Formally, this asks for a method that verifies functional completion — e.g., closure, seal integrity, absence of retained material — and rules out hidden damage created by the procedure itself.
status: Autonomous anastomosis and learned surgical tasks provide important demonstrations; functional verification remains a separate requirement. Key works: Saeidi et al. (2022), *Autonomous robotic laparoscopic surgery for intestinal anastomosis*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abj2908; Kim et al. (2024), *Surgical Robot Transformer*, arXiv:2407.12998.
solved_when: A robotic system can, without human judgment, verify that a surgical step achieved its intended physiological outcome and detect hidden damage such as incomplete closure, leaks, retained material, or incorrect tissue handling, using only measurements available during the procedure.
why: Detects incomplete closure, leaks, retained material, or incorrect tissue handling — the failure modes that instrument-motion-based evaluation silently misses, and the ones most dangerous to the patient.
key_works: Saeidi et al. (2022), *Autonomous robotic laparoscopic surgery for intestinal anastomosis*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abj2908; Kim et al. (2024), *Surgical Robot Transformer*, arXiv:2407.12998.

title: Needle steering with uncertain tissue motion
open: Can an autonomous needle-steering system reliably reach anatomical targets and avoid critical structures even when tissue deforms, moves physiologically during the procedure, and differs materially from preoperative models?
status: Autonomous medical needle steering has been demonstrated in vivo (Kuntz et al. (2023), *Autonomous medical needle steering in vivo*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adf7614), but robust transfer across anatomical and motion conditions remains a broader target; AI guidance for medical motion planning is surveyed in Alterovitz et al., *A Review of AI Guidance for Medical Motion Planning*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-032024-024305.
solved_when: A steering method is demonstrated that reaches targets while avoiding critical structures under tissue deformation, physiological motion, and deviations from preoperative models, with robust transfer across anatomical and motion conditions.
why: It improves minimally invasive access to targets that are difficult to reach, making percutaneous procedures safer and more widely applicable.
key_works: Kuntz et al. (2023), *Autonomous medical needle steering in vivo*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adf7614; Alterovitz et al., *A Review of AI Guidance for Medical Motion Planning*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-032024-024305.

title: Predicting collateral thermal damage
open: Can a robotic energy-based treatment system estimate and control thermal injury beneath the tissue surface while tissue properties, perfusion, and sensor visibility remain uncertain?
status: Surgical autonomy currently integrates sensing and control, but visible tool placement alone cannot certify thermal effects; related directions include inverse bioheat transfer and thermal-dose estimation. Key work: Attanasio et al. (2021), *Autonomy in Surgical Robotics*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-062420-090543.
solved_when: An experimental system demonstrates estimation and control of subsurface thermal injury during robotic energy-based treatment under uncertain tissue properties, perfusion, and sensor visibility, protecting structures outside the immediate treatment target.
why: Structures outside the immediate treatment target — nerves, vessels, and other vulnerable anatomy — are put at risk by thermal spread that the surgeon cannot directly observe; predicting collateral damage is what makes energy-based robotic surgery safe around them.
key_works: Attanasio et al. (2021), *Autonomy in Surgical Robotics*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-062420-090543.

title: Recovery from unexpected bleeding or tissue failure
open: When an unexpected event such as bleeding or tissue failure interrupts a planned surgical step, can an autonomous system detect the deviation, stabilize the patient's condition, and execute a validated fallback while preserving clinician control?
status: SRT-H (Kim et al. (2025), *SRT-H*, arXiv:2505.10251) advances multistep autonomy in surgery, but emergency recovery remains a separately demonstrated safety capability that has not yet been shown.
solved_when: A system demonstrates, on a validated surgical task, detection of a deviation from the planned step, stabilization of the situation, execution of a validated fallback behavior, and preservation of clinician control throughout the recovery.
why: These are the failures that matter most clinically; without demonstrated emergency recovery, autonomous surgical systems cannot be trusted on the steps where deviation is most dangerous.
key_works: Kim et al. (2025), *SRT-H*, arXiv:2505.10251.

title: Surgical training data with realistic rare complications
open: Can we create ethically collected, richly annotated surgical datasets that capture the rare and difficult cases — complications, interventions, anatomical variation, and failed attempts — rather than only successful nominal procedures?
status: SRT demonstrates learning from surgical demonstrations, but rare-event coverage and intervention provenance remain additional dataset requirements (Kim et al. (2024), *Surgical Robot Transformer: Imitation Learning for Surgical Tasks*, arXiv:2407.12998).
solved_when: A publicly documented dataset exists that is ethically collected and well annotated, and that includes coverage of rare complications, interventions, anatomical variation, and failed attempts, not just successful nominal procedures.
why: Such data enables evaluation of failure handling without relying on unsafe trial-and-error on real patients.
key_works: Kim et al. (2024), *Surgical Robot Transformer: Imitation Learning for Surgical Tasks*, arXiv:2407.12998.

title: Clinical evidence for increasing surgical autonomy
open: How can clinical trials be designed so that the benefits and harms of a surgical robot are attributed specifically to its autonomous component rather than to the system as a whole? Such designs must also capture escalation behavior, operator workload, and changes observed after market release.
status: A 2024 study classified autonomy in FDA-cleared robots over its historical study period, and it distinguishes laboratory capability from clinical authorization as separate evidence questions. Key work: Lee et al. (2024), *Levels of autonomy in FDA-cleared surgical robots*, DOI:10.1038/s41746-024-01102-y.
solved_when: Trial designs and validated outcome measures exist that causally attribute clinical benefit and harm to the autonomous component itself, including metrics for escalation, operator workload, and post-market changes.
why: It underpins a responsible transition from experimental autonomy to routine clinical practice; without valid attribution, neither regulators nor surgeons can know whether autonomy itself helps or harms patients.
key_works: Lee et al. (2024), *Levels of autonomy in FDA-cleared surgical robots*, DOI:10.1038/s41746-024-01102-y.

title: Safe feeding across variable food and user states
open: How can a robot safely feed a person — acquiring, transporting, and presenting a wide variety of foods while continuously adapting to the user's motion and readiness to bite? A complete answer must explicitly account for spill risk, failed bites, and swallowing-related limits across both food and user states.
status: Current haptic food-manipulation research addresses the acquisition stage, e.g. Bhattacharjee et al. (2019), *Towards Robotic Feeding: Role of Haptics in Fork-Based Food Manipulation*, IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 4(2):1485–1492; complete safe assistance additionally requires user-state and delivery reasoning.
solved_when: An assistive feeding system exists that can acquire, transport, and present diverse foods while adapting in real time to user motion and readiness, with explicit mechanisms for handling spills, failed bites, and swallowing-related limits.
why: It would support greater independence during meals for people who cannot feed themselves.
key_works: Bhattacharjee et al. (2019), *Towards Robotic Feeding: Role of Haptics in Fork-Based Food Manipulation*, IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 4(2):1485–1492.

title: Patient transfer with uncertain body support
open: Can an assistive robot safely transfer a patient between a bed, a chair, and standing while simultaneously inferring the patient's load distribution, level of participation, pain, and balance — without resorting to probing actions that could themselves be unsafe?
status: Safe physical human-robot interaction supplies relevant methods — see Lasota, Fong, and Shah (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052 — but transfer assistance additionally demands whole-body support and constraints tailored to the individual.
solved_when: A robot system demonstrates transfers between bed, chair, and standing positions while inferring load distribution, user participation, pain, and balance from safe, non-probing interaction, respecting whole-body support and individualized constraints.
why: Successful inference and control during transfer directly reduces injury risk for both users and caregivers.
key_works: Lasota, Fong, and Shah (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052.

title: Exoskeleton assistance across real-world transitions
open: Can an assistive exoskeleton adapt its support continuously through the transitions of daily life — stairs, slopes, turning, speed changes, stopping, and irregular surfaces — without ever destabilizing the wearer? Formally, this asks for control and personalization methods that maintain stability and assistance benefit across non-steady, non-treadmill locomotion.
status: Real-world personalization of assistance has been demonstrated; reliable transitions across diverse daily activities remain a broader target. Key work: Slade et al. (2022), *Personalizing exoskeleton assistance while walking in the real world*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-022-05191-1.
solved_when: Assistance is adapted through all of stairs, slopes, turning, speed changes, stopping, and irregular surfaces without destabilizing the wearer, across diverse daily activities.
why: It would extend the demonstrated benefits of exoskeleton assistance beyond steady treadmill walking into the real world, where users actually live and move.
key_works: Slade et al. (2022), *Personalizing exoskeleton assistance while walking in the real world*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-022-05191-1.

title: Personalization for changing impairment and fatigue
open: How can an assistive device adapt its assistance in real time as a user's strength, fatigue, pain, and recovery change over time, without requiring burdensome repeated laboratory calibration sessions?
status: Human-in-the-loop optimization has demonstrated individualized walking assistance (Zhang et al. (2017), *Human-in-the-loop optimization of exoskeleton assistance during walking*, DOI:10.1126/science.aal5054), but clinical use and time-varying personalization introduce additional constraints.
solved_when: A personalization method is demonstrated that tracks a user's evolving physical state and maintains optimized assistance across those changes, while avoiding repeated laboratory calibration.
why: It makes assistance responsive to the individual person rather than a fixed average model.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2017), *Human-in-the-loop optimization of exoskeleton assistance during walking*, DOI:10.1126/science.aal5054.

title: Stable neural control over months and years
open: Can a prosthetic or robotic control system remain stable and usable over months and years of use, even as neural signals, electrode interfaces, user strategies, and physiological state all drift and change?
status: Brain–computer interfaces already demonstrate meaningful robotic control and sensory feedback, but long-term stability remains a distinct translational target. A key demonstration is Flesher et al. (2021), *A brain-computer interface that evokes tactile sensations improves robotic arm control*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd0380.
solved_when: A brain–computer-interface-driven prosthetic or robotic controller maintains meaningful control and sensory feedback over months to years without requiring repeated recalibration, tolerating changes in neural signals, electrode interfaces, user strategies, and physiological state.
why: It would cut the recalibration burden that currently makes assistive functions unreliable to access, turning laboratory demonstrations into dependable daily tools for users.
key_works: Flesher et al. (2021), *A brain-computer interface that evokes tactile sensations improves robotic arm control*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd0380.

title: Useful artificial touch beyond laboratory tasks
open: Deliver tactile feedback that consistently improves everyday manipulation, embodiment, and safety across users and object classes.
status: Evoked tactile sensations improved robotic arm control in a published BCI study (Flesher et al. (2021), *A brain-computer interface that evokes tactile sensations improves robotic arm control*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd0380); broad daily-life benefit requires additional evidence.
solved_when: Artificial touch is shown to reliably improve manipulation performance, embodiment, and safety for users across diverse users and object classes in everyday settings, not just laboratory tasks.
why: Restores information essential to natural dexterity.
key_works: Flesher et al. (2021), *A brain-computer interface that evokes tactile sensations improves robotic arm control*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd0380.

title: Assistive robots that remain useful after deployment
open: Can assistive robots remain genuinely useful over sustained home use, once the realities of deployment are counted? The challenge is to demonstrate real-world durability while accounting for setup, cleaning, repairs, caregiver effort, abandonment, and changing user needs.
status: The WHO–UNICEF assistive-technology report documents broader access and service challenges; robot-specific longitudinal service models require evidence. Key work: WHO and UNICEF (2022), *Global Report on Assistive Technology*, ISBN:9789240049451.
solved_when: A demonstration of sustained home use is achieved with explicit accounting of setup, cleaning, repairs, caregiver effort, abandonment, and changing user needs — i.e., evidence-backed longitudinal service models for assistive robots, not just laboratory capability.
why: It ensures that technical capability translates into durable independence for users; without it, robots that work in demos fail in homes.
key_works: WHO and UNICEF (2022), *Global Report on Assistive Technology*, ISBN:9789240049451.

title: Legible motion for diverse observers
open: Can a robot generate motion that communicates its intent to observers who differ in experience, culture, attention, and physical ability? Formally, the goal is motion generation that stays legible across such observer diversity without sacrificing safety or task feasibility.
status: Legibility and predictability of robot motion were distinguished experimentally by Dragan, Lee, and Srinivasa (2013), *Legibility and predictability of robot motion*, IEEE ICRA; generalization across users and contexts remains a broader target.
solved_when: A motion-generation method demonstrably produces motions that communicate intent across diverse observers — varying in experience, culture, attention, and physical ability — while preserving safety and task feasibility.
why: It reduces surprise for human observers and improves human–robot coordination.
key_works: Dragan, Lee, and Srinivasa (2013), *Legibility and predictability of robot motion*, IEEE ICRA.

title: Trust calibrated to actual robot competence
open: Can users' trust in a robot be calibrated to track the robot's actual competence as it changes, so that reliance rises and falls appropriately rather than trust or perceived friendliness simply being maximized?
status: A 2024 review by Haney and Liang, *A literature review on safety perception and trust during human-robot interaction with autonomous mobile robots that apply to industrial environments* (DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537), identifies measurement and field-validation gaps in safety perception and trust.
solved_when: An experimental method demonstrates that user reliance on a robot matches its measured, changing competence — avoiding both overreliance and unnecessary rejection — with validated measurement and field validation.
why: Prevents both dangerous overreliance and unnecessary rejection of robotic systems.
key_works: Haney and Liang (2024), *A literature review on safety perception and trust during human-robot interaction with autonomous mobile robots that apply to industrial environments*, DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537.

title: Field-valid measures of perceived and actual safety
open: Can we build measures of safety in human–robot interaction that distinguish feeling safe from actually being safe, and that predict real behavior during prolonged real-world interaction?
status: A 2024 review (Haney and Liang (2024), *A literature review on safety perception and trust…*, DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537) found predominantly controlled laboratory experiments and limited industrial-platform coverage.
solved_when: Validated measures exist that (i) separate perceived from actual safety and (ii) demonstrably predict behavior in prolonged real-world interaction, not just laboratory settings.
why: Without such measures, improvements in questionnaire scores can be mistaken for reductions in actual harm.
key_works: Haney and Liang (2024), *A literature review on safety perception and trust…*, DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537.

title: Human interaction with multiple simultaneous robots
open: How can coordination and signaling among multiple robots be designed so that nearby humans can still understand what the robots are doing when several act simultaneously around them? More precisely, what coordination and signaling schemes preserve human understandability under concurrent multi-robot motion and action?
status: Human–robot safety methods largely address individual human–robot interactions; extending to combined robot behavior introduces problems of human attention allocation and predictability. Lasota et al. (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052.
solved_when: A coordination and signaling design is demonstrated (experimentally) to remain understandable to humans in settings where multiple robots move and act simultaneously around them.
why: It enables safe deployment of genuine robot fleets in warehouses, hospitals, and public spaces.
key_works: Lasota et al. (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052.

title: Negotiating autonomy and consent during tasks
open: How can a user grant, limit, revise, or revoke a robot's task authority mid-task, in a form the robot can interpret and enforce while the physical work is still underway? Formally, this asks for an interaction protocol and robot-side representation of delegated authority that remains valid and enforceable as consent changes during ongoing work.
status: Language-grounded affordance systems, such as Ahn et al. (2022), *Do As I Can, Not As I Say*, arXiv:2204.01691, support instruction following, but authority negotiation requires more than selecting an executable skill.
solved_when: A working system exists in which users can issue and revoke authority grants during active physical tasks, and the robot correctly interprets and enforces these changes in real time without halting or restarting the task.
why: It preserves meaningful user control over robots acting in the physical world; without enforceable revocation, delegation during teleoperation becomes an all-or-nothing commitment the user cannot safely walk back.
key_works: Ahn et al. (2022), *Do As I Can, Not As I Say*, arXiv:2204.01691.

title: Transparent teleoperation over variable networks
open: Can a teleoperation system deliver convincing force and motion feedback to the human operator across a network whose delay, packet loss, and dynamics vary over time and are only partially modeled, without ever losing stability? Formally, the goal is a bilateral controller that jointly guarantees stability and high transparency under variable delay, packet loss, and model mismatch.
status: Passivity-based methods solved important delay-stability problems, beginning with Anderson and Spong (1989), *Bilateral control of teleoperators with time delay*, DOI:10.1109/9.24201, and extended to time-varying delay by Wang (2021), *Bilateral control of teleoperator systems with time-varying delay*, DOI:10.1016/j.automatica.2021.109707. Nonetheless, achieving high transparency under realistic network and contact conditions remains a tradeoff.
solved_when: A bilateral teleoperation scheme is specified that preserves stability while achieving convincing force and motion transparency under variable delay, packet loss, and model mismatch — since the record states no quantitative budgets (round counts, exponents, or sizes), the natural criterion for this problem type applies.
why: It would enable effective remote intervention over real networks while keeping dangerous contact forces perceptible to the operator rather than masked by the controller.
key_works: Anderson and Spong (1989), *Bilateral control of teleoperators with time delay*, DOI:10.1109/9.24201; Wang (2021), *Bilateral control of teleoperator systems with time-varying delay*, DOI:10.1016/j.automatica.2021.109707.

title: Handover timing under uncertain human readiness
open: When should a robot release or transfer an object to a human whose readiness cannot be observed directly? The goal is a handover controller that transfers the load only when the human is actually ready and supporting it, while remaining robust to distraction, hesitation, weakness, or unexpected withdrawal.
status: Safe physical human–robot interaction offers relevant sensing and control methods, but readiness in this setting is a hidden human state rather than a fixed trajectory event, so existing trajectory-based approaches do not directly solve the timing problem. Key work: Lasota et al. (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052.
solved_when: A controller exists that achieves safe, comfortable object handovers in which release occurs only when the human is ready and supporting the load, correctly handling distraction, hesitation, weakness, and unexpected withdrawal during the interaction.
why: It would make routine physical collaboration between humans and robots comfortable and safe, rather than requiring the human to conform to a fixed robot schedule.
key_works: Lasota et al. (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052.

title: Long-term psychosocial effects of social robots
open: Which patterns of repeated interaction with social robots lead to lasting psychosocial benefits or harms? A satisfactory answer must isolate genuine causal effects from novelty effects, selection bias, and the displacement of human contact.
status: Social interaction and ethics were identified among robotics' grand challenges in Yang et al. (2018), *The grand challenges of Science Robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aar7650; longitudinal causal evidence remains the appropriate target and has not yet been established.
solved_when: Longitudinal causal evidence identifies which forms of repeated social-robot interaction produce durable benefits or harms, with novelty effects, selection bias, and displacement of human contact separated out.
why: It prevents adoption decisions from being driven solely by short-term engagement, which may not reflect durable effects on people's psychosocial well-being.
key_works: Yang et al. (2018), *The grand challenges of Science Robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aar7650.

title: Open-world road-scene understanding
open: Can a road-scene understanding system reliably detect and reason about what its training data never anticipated — unusual road configurations, temporary instructions, debris, emergency activity, and objects outside its training taxonomy — rather than only the closed set of categories it was trained on?
status: Autonomous-driving systems have mature perception pipelines; uncommon combinations and open-set conditions remain fundamental challenges (Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving: Common Practices and Emerging Technologies*, arXiv:1906.05113).
solved_when: A driving-perception system is demonstrated that handles open-set road conditions — novel object categories, temporary signals, and anomalous scene configurations — with a quantified failure rate on such conditions, without the record's specific numeric targets (none are stated), the natural criterion is performance on open-world conditions not represented in ordinary object-detection benchmarks.
why: It addresses failure modes that ordinary object-detection benchmarks do not represent, which is where real-world autonomy actually breaks down.
key_works: Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving: Common Practices and Emerging Technologies*, arXiv:1906.05113.

title: Joint uncertainty over interacting road users
open: Can we predict the futures of multiple interacting road users with calibrated joint distributions that preserve dependence among agents and respond correctly to the ego vehicle’s actions? In formal terms, the goal is joint, interaction-aware forecasting whose counterfactual predictions shift appropriately with the ego vehicle’s planned behavior.
status: Large motion-forecasting datasets support interaction modeling, as reflected in Ettinger et al. (2021), *Large Scale Interactive Motion Forecasting for Autonomous Driving: The Waymo Open Motion Dataset*, arXiv:2104.10133; accurate joint counterfactual prediction is stronger than marginal trajectory prediction.
solved_when: A forecasting method produces calibrated joint distributions over multi-agent futures that preserve inter-agent dependence and yield accurate counterfactual predictions conditioned on the ego vehicle’s actions, demonstrating that joint counterfactual prediction is stronger than marginal trajectory prediction.
why: It prevents planners from combining individually plausible but mutually inconsistent agent futures, which would otherwise lead to unsafe or incoherent plans.
key_works: Ettinger et al. (2021), *Large Scale Interactive Motion Forecasting for Autonomous Driving: The Waymo Open Motion Dataset*, arXiv:2104.10133.

title: Negotiation without aggressive or exploitable behavior
open: How should an autonomous vehicle merge, cross, or yield when the human drivers around it adapt their behavior to its presence? The question is whether a policy exists that interacts effectively in such settings without becoming dangerously assertive or indefinitely passive.
status: Interactive driving is widely studied, but guarantees under uncertain human response remain challenging. Related: games with incomplete information; equilibrium selection. Key works: Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:1906.05113.
solved_when: A policy or theoretical framework is established for interactive driving (merging, crossing, yielding) that remains effective under uncertain, adaptive human responses while provably avoiding both overly aggressive and indefinitely passive behavior.
