why: It would make autonomous vehicles socially functional participants in mixed traffic, rather than agents that either bully or freeze when humans react to them.
key_works: Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:1906.05113.

title: Risk-aware handling of occluded road users
open: How should an autonomous vehicle choose its speed and lateral position when pedestrians or other vehicles may be hidden behind occlusions, without assuming worst-case adversarial behavior at every blind spot? A principled answer would couple a calibrated model of occluded-agent uncertainty with a driving policy that trades caution against progress.
status: Multimodal driving datasets improve visible-scene understanding; occluded-agent risk requires additional models and validation. Key works: Caesar et al. (2020), *nuScenes: A multimodal dataset for autonomous driving*, arXiv:1903.11027.
solved_when: A decision-making framework exists that provably or demonstrably selects speed and position using quantified uncertainty about unseen road users, avoids the assumption that every occlusion hides an adversarial actor, and is validated on realistic driving scenarios.
why: It balances safety against usable progress: overly conservative occlusion handling stalls the vehicle, while ignoring unseen agents risks collisions with vulnerable road users.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2020), *nuScenes: A multimodal dataset for autonomous driving*, arXiv:1903.11027.

title: Statistically credible rare-event safety validation
open: How can we demonstrate that an autonomous vehicle has acceptably low serious-failure rates without either driving an infeasibly large number of undifferentiated road miles or extrapolating from unvalidated simulation? Formally, the question is how to combine and statistically validate evidence from multiple sources so that rare-event safety claims become credible.
status: Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to safety: How many miles of driving would it take to demonstrate autonomous vehicle reliability?*, DOI:10.1016/j.tra.2016.09.010, quantified the limitations of mileage-based reliability demonstrations; combining evidence sources remains an important open problem.
solved_when: A validation methodology exists that yields statistically credible bounds on serious-failure rates at realistic cost, without relying on infeasibly large undifferentiated mileage totals or unvalidated simulation extrapolation.
why: It makes safety claims testable at realistic cost.
key_works: Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to safety: How many miles of driving would it take to demonstrate autonomous vehicle reliability?*, DOI:10.1016/j.tra.2016.09.010.

title: Sensor-fusion robustness under adverse weather
open: Can an autonomous vehicle's perception stack maintain accurate calibration and reliable sensing when rain, snow, fog, glare, dirt, and spray degrade several sensors at once in correlated ways? More formally, the goal is to preserve calibrated multimodal perception under simultaneous, correlated common-cause environmental disturbances across sensors.
status: Multimodal datasets provide important baselines, but sensor diversity does not eliminate common environmental failure modes. Key works: Caesar et al. (2020), *nuScenes*, arXiv:1903.11027.
solved_when: A perception system maintains calibration and detection performance under simultaneous adverse conditions (rain, snow, fog, glare, dirt, spray) affecting multiple sensors in correlated ways, with no single environmental factor causing failure.
why: It expands the dependable operating conditions of autonomous vehicles beyond fair weather, which is required for deployment in real climates.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2020), *nuScenes*, arXiv:1903.11027.

title: Safe fallback when stopping is itself hazardous
open: When an autonomous vehicle detects a failure, how should it choose the safest fallback maneuver — given that coming to an immediate stop could itself cause a collision or strand the vehicle in an unsafe spot?
status: Autonomous-driving architectures already include fallback behavior, but appropriate risk minimization depends on traffic, road geometry, and remaining capabilities. Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:1906.05113.
solved_when: The system selects a minimum-risk response to failure that accounts for surrounding traffic, road geometry, and the vehicle's remaining capabilities, rather than defaulting to an immediate stop.
why: It makes system-failure handling context-sensitive instead of relying on a fixed stop, so degraded vehicles degrade gracefully in real traffic conditions.
key_works: Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:1906.05113.

title: Cooperative driving with untrusted or missing infrastructure data
open: How can an autonomous vehicle exploit cooperative messages from other vehicles and roadside infrastructure while remaining safe when those messages are delayed, incorrect, unavailable, or inconsistent with its own onboard observations? Formally, the question is to design a cooperative driving system whose safety does not degrade below the safety of a purely autonomous baseline whenever external data is untrusted or missing.
status: Interactive motion modeling and connected operation offer benefits, but dependence on external information creates additional uncertainty and security constraints. Related directions include resilient distributed estimation and authenticated sensor fusion; a key work is Ettinger et al. (2021), *Large Scale Interactive Motion Forecasting for Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:2104.10133.
solved_when: A cooperative driving method is demonstrated that uses vehicle and infrastructure messages for benefit, yet provably or demonstrably maintains safety when messages are delayed, incorrect, unavailable, or inconsistent with onboard observations.
why: It enables cooperation without making connectivity a safety prerequisite, so vehicles can gain the benefits of interactive motion modeling and connected operation without introducing new uncertainty and security constraints as failure points.
key_works: Ettinger et al. (2021), *Large Scale Interactive Motion Forecasting for Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:2104.10133.

title: Benchmarks that measure intervention-free completion
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Can we evaluate complete robotic workflows in a way that counts every reset, teleoperation episode, scene adjustment, and human recovery action as part of the score?
status: FurnitureBench offers reproducible long-horizon physical tasks; an intervention-complete accounting standard is an additional requirement. Key work: Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench*, arXiv:2305.12821.
solved_when: A benchmark exists that measures full workflows while systematically counting every reset, teleoperation episode, scene adjustment, and human recovery action, so that reported scores reflect intervention-free completion.
why: It makes benchmark scores comparable to actual autonomous usefulness, rather than crediting policies for performance that silently depends on human labor.
key_works: Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench*, arXiv:2305.12821.

title: Robot-data provenance with physically meaningful metadata
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Can the provenance of robot datasets be captured in a standardized, machine-checkable form that records the facts a physical system actually depends on? In particular, can calibration, embodiment, control mode, operator intervention, sensor timing, licensing, and environmental conditions be encoded as first-class provenance metadata?
status: Datasheets (Gebru et al. (2021), *Datasheets for Datasets*, arXiv:1803.09010) establish a general documentation framework, but robotic data require additional physical and temporal semantics; large-scale efforts such as Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2023), *Open X-Embodiment*, arXiv:2310.08864, highlight the need for cross-embodiment provenance.
solved_when: A provenance schema exists that records calibration, embodiment, control mode, operator intervention, sensor timing, licensing, and environmental conditions in machine-checkable form, and is adopted for robot datasets.
why: It supports trustworthy reuse of robot data and enables principled diagnosis of transfer failures when a policy or model moves between embodiments and environments.
key_works: Gebru et al. (2021), *Datasheets for Datasets*, arXiv:1803.09010; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2023), *Open X-Embodiment*, arXiv:2310.08864.

title: Simulator rankings that predict physical rankings
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: When does a method's ranking on a simulator benchmark actually predict its ranking on real robots? A formal account should also quantify uncertainty over rank reversals between simulation and physical deployment.
status: Simulation suites such as SoftGym support controlled comparisons; predictive validity for physical deployment requires paired experiments (Lin et al. (2020), *SoftGym*, arXiv:2011.07215).
solved_when: A validation methodology (e.g., paired simulator–robot experiments) exists that can establish — with quantified uncertainty over rank reversals — when simulator benchmark rankings transfer to physical rankings.
why: Without it, practitioners risk optimizing benchmarks that select the wrong methods for deployment, wasting effort on methods that win in simulation but fail on hardware.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), *SoftGym*, arXiv:2011.07215.

title: Shared corpora of failures and recoveries
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Can the robotics community assemble a shared corpus of robot failures — including failed attempts, near misses, operator interventions, and successful recoveries — annotated with enough context to study why failures happen and how systems recover?
status: DROID (Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID*, arXiv:2403.12945) expands real-world manipulation data, but a failure-centered corpus has different sampling and annotation requirements and does not yet exist.
solved_when: A publicly shared dataset exists that captures representative failures and recoveries with the contextual annotations needed to support research on failure mechanisms.
why: Such a corpus enables the study of reliability rather than only imitation of successful behavior, which is what current success-only datasets support.
key_works: Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID*, arXiv:2403.12945.

title: Public contact and wear reference datasets
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Can the community assemble and publish a shared reference dataset of contact and wear that is rich enough to validate simulators and tactile sensors against each other? Concretely, this means synchronized measurements of force, geometry, material, environmental, and degradation signals captured on the same physical interactions.
status: Contact-model comparisons — e.g., Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372 — establish the importance of modeling choices; broad physical reference data would make those comparisons more decisive.
solved_when: A publicly released dataset exists containing synchronized force, geometry, material, environmental, and degradation measurements, and it demonstrably supports cross-simulator and cross-sensor validation.
why: Such a dataset anchors simulation and tactile learning to measured mechanics, turning qualitative comparisons of contact models into decisive ones.
key_works: Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372.

title: End-to-end real-time guarantees for modern robot stacks
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Can we bound the sensing-to-actuation latency of a complete modern robot stack — neural inference, middleware, logging, networking, and multiple controllers sharing heterogeneous processors — with end-to-end worst-case guarantees rather than per-component measurements?
status: ROS 2 addresses production-oriented middleware requirements, but application-wide worst-case timing still requires additional analysis. Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2: Design, Architecture, and Uses In The Wild*, arXiv:2211.07752.
solved_when: A robot stack of this kind carries a provable end-to-end worst-case latency bound from sensing to actuation that holds under actual system load, covering neural inference, middleware, logging, networking, and multiple controllers on heterogeneous processors.
why: Control designs assume their timing deadlines are met; without an end-to-end bound those assumptions can fail under real system load, destabilizing controllers even when every component is individually fast.
key_works: Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2: Design, Architecture, and Uses In The Wild*, arXiv:2211.07752.

title: Portable skill interfaces with executable contracts
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Can robot skills be specified as portable, machine-checkable interfaces that any platform can execute correctly? In particular, define skill descriptions that expose preconditions, effects, uncertainty, resource needs, authority requirements, and recovery behavior in a form that transfers across robot platforms.
status: Generalist datasets and policies already share experience across platforms (e.g., Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2023), *Open X-Embodiment*, arXiv:2310.08864), but portable execution semantics require more than common action tensors; related formal machinery exists in contract-based software composition, typed effect systems, and PDDLStream (Garrett et al. (2020), arXiv:1802.08705), yet no cross-platform executable skill contract standard is established.
solved_when: A skill interface specification exists that captures preconditions, effects, uncertainty, resource needs, authority requirements, and recovery behavior, and skills written against it execute correctly across different robot platforms without platform-specific redefinition.
why: It eliminates repeated per-platform integration work while preserving correctness guarantees, so generalist policies can share skills rather than merely sharing action tensors.
key_works: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2023), *Open X-Embodiment*, arXiv:2310.08864; Garrett et al. (2020), *PDDLStream*, arXiv:1802.08705.

title: Accessible shared physical evaluation facilities
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Can the robotics community establish shared, remotely accessible physical evaluation facilities so that any researcher can test on real robots without owning a laboratory? Concretely, this means independently operated testbeds with maintained hardware, standardized reset procedures, and transparent queueing and cost structures.
status: Open datasets lower one access barrier, but independent physical replication still requires equipment and operational support. Key works include Chi et al. (2024), *Universal Manipulation Interface*, arXiv:2402.10329; Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID*, arXiv:2403.12945.
solved_when: Such facilities exist and are operational: remotely accessible, independently operated, with maintained hardware, standardized resets, and transparent queueing and costs.
why: It allows more researchers to test claims on real hardware without building duplicate laboratories.
key_works: Chi et al. (2024), *Universal Manipulation Interface*, arXiv:2402.10329; Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID*, arXiv:2403.12945.

title: Cybersecurity metrics that reflect physical consequences
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: How should robotic vulnerabilities be scored by the physical harm they could cause, rather than by conventional software severity alone? A satisfactory framework would quantify potential physical harm, recoverability, exposure, and compensating controls in a unified metric.
status: Robotics cybersecurity research advocates robot-specific risk assessment, but calibrated models of physical consequence remain to be developed. Key work: Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems: Leading Challenges and Robotic System Design Methodology*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850.
solved_when: A calibrated quantitative metric for robotic vulnerabilities is established that incorporates potential physical harm, recoverability, exposure, and compensating controls, going beyond conventional software severity scores.
why: It allows defenders to prioritize protections for people and equipment, rather than treating robot breaches like ordinary software flaws.
key_works: Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems: Leading Challenges and Robotic System Design Methodology*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850.

title: Enforceable authority boundaries for language-controlled robots
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Can a language-controlled robot be built so that no text, image, external document, or third-party message can ever authorize physical actions beyond the user’s current permissions? Formally, is there an enforcement architecture in which unauthenticated channels influence task content but never capability?
status: Language-generated robot programs expand interfaces, so secure delegation must distinguish task content from authenticated authority. Related directions include prompt-injection resistance and capability-based security. Key works: Liang et al. (2022), *Code as Policies*, arXiv:2209.07753; Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850.
solved_when: A working robot system demonstrates that all inputs from text, images, external documents, and third-party messages are confined to the user’s current permission set, with no such input able to trigger physical actions beyond it.
why: It prevents untrusted observations from becoming commands, closing the gap by which language-generated robot programs expand the attack surface of physical systems.
key_works: Liang et al. (2022), *Code as Policies*, arXiv:2209.07753; Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850.

title: Security updates that preserve physical safety
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: How can long-lived robots receive security patches without compromising the physical behaviors that keep them safe? The goal is an update process that preserves timing, calibration, and control behavior, and retains the ability to roll back — even when an update is interrupted mid-deployment.
status: Robot cybersecurity and production middleware each address parts of the problem, but composing security assurance with safety assurance remains open. Key works: Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850; Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2*, arXiv:2211.07752.
solved_when: A deployable update mechanism exists that applies security patches to long-lived robots while preserving timing, calibration, and control behavior, maintains rollback capability, and correctly handles interrupted updates.
why: Without it, operators must choose between running vulnerable software and accepting unvalidated changes to safety-critical behavior; a solution removes that trade-off.
key_works: Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850; Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2*, arXiv:2211.07752.

title: Privacy-preserving robot incident reporting
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Can robots and robot-operating organizations report injuries, near misses, interventions, and failures to a shared, interoperable system without exposing people, confidential environments, or legitimate proprietary information? In other words, what data schemas and privacy mechanisms make incident reporting both reusable across organizations and privacy-preserving by design?
status: NIOSH's robotics program studies occupational risks; the proposed target extends surveillance into reusable, privacy-preserving incident data.
solved_when: An interoperable incident-reporting mechanism exists that captures injuries, near misses, interventions, and failures in a reusable form while demonstrably protecting people, confidential environments, and legitimate proprietary information.
why: It allows the field to learn from failures that individual organizations may rarely observe on their own.
key_works: NIOSH (2024), *Center for Occupational Robotics Research*; Gebru et al. (2021), *Datasheets for Datasets*, arXiv:1803.09010.

title: Durable funding for independent long-term replication
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: How can we finance and reward independent, multi-month replication efforts — including maintenance reporting and negative results — in robotics? The goal is to design durable funding mechanisms and publication incentives that make such replication a sustainable public good rather than an occasional act of goodwill.
status: Risk-management frameworks currently emphasize measurement and monitoring — e.g. NIST (2023), *Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)*, DOI:10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1 — but sustained independent robotic replication remains a proposed public-good target; no quantified claim is made that zero funding exists today.
solved_when: A working financing and incentive scheme exists under which independent teams can carry out multi-month robotic replications, report on system maintenance, and publish negative results, with those outputs institutionally funded and recognized for publication.
why: It would make replication routine enough to test whether reported robotic capabilities actually survive transfer to different teams and operating conditions, rather than being validated only by their original authors.
key_works: NIST (2023), *Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)*, DOI:10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1.

title: Repairability and end-of-life support for deployed robots
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: How can deployed robots be kept serviceable — and safely retired — after their vendors or product lines disappear? The goal is to develop sustainable technical and commercial arrangements for spare parts, calibration data, security maintenance, and safe end-of-life support for fielded systems.
status: Robotics' grand challenges are usually framed around materials, power, and societal integration; this target instead concerns lifetime support rather than initial capability, as surveyed in Yang et al. (2018), *The grand challenges of Science Robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aar7650.
solved_when: Workable arrangements exist that supply spare parts, calibration data, and security maintenance, and govern safe retirement, for robots whose vendors or product lines have disappeared, so that such systems remain usable and safe rather than stranded.
why: Without such arrangements, expensive robots become unusable or unsafe stranded assets once vendor support ends.
key_works: Yang et al. (2018), *The grand challenges of Science Robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aar7650.

title: Evidence and payment models for useful assistive robots
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: How can procurement and reimbursement models be designed so that they reward measured independence, caregiver burden reduction, reliability, and ongoing service rather than device purchase alone?
status: WHO and UNICEF document assistive-technology access and service challenges in *Global Report on Assistive Technology* (WHO and UNICEF (2022), ISBN:9789240049451), but robot-specific outcome and payment evidence remains necessary.
solved_when: Payment or procurement models exist that tie reimbursement to measured outcomes — user independence, caregiver burden reduction, reliability, and sustained service — instead of compensating only the upfront device purchase.
why: Such models connect effective assistive technology to users who cannot finance experimental products out of pocket, so proven technology actually reaches the people who need it.
key_works: WHO and UNICEF (2022), *Global Report on Assistive Technology*, ISBN:9789240049451.

title: Worker participation in robotic deployment decisions
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: How can workers who are affected by robotic deployment be given meaningful influence over decisions about task allocation, monitoring, safety controls, training, and recourse — and can such participatory deployment processes be validated in practice?
status: Occupational robotics research addresses emerging workplace risks; the unresolved target is a validated participatory deployment model. Key works: NIOSH (2024), *Center for Occupational Robotics Research*; NIST (2023), *AI Risk Management Framework 1.0*.
solved_when: A participatory deployment model covering task allocation, monitoring, safety controls, training, and recourse has been developed and empirically evaluated, yielding a validated deployment process.
why: It improves the chance that workplace automation delivers shared benefits rather than merely shifting risk onto affected workers.
key_works: NIOSH (2024), *Center for Occupational Robotics Research*; NIST (2023), *AI Risk Management Framework 1.0*.
